content:
## What Soundraw Actually Does (From a Freelance Video Editor's Desk)

I cut short-form video for a few small brands and two YouTube channels. For years the background-music part of the job was a quiet tax: I would burn an hour hunting royalty-free tracks on paid libraries, only to get a copyright claim six months later because the "free" track was never actually cleared. Soundraw ended that specific headache for me in late 2024, and I have billed it into client work ever since.

Here is the plain version. Soundraw is an AI music generator. You pick a genre, a mood, a length, and an intensity, and it returns an original track - not a sample grabbed off the internet, but a piece composed by a model trained only on music its own team wrote and recorded. That detail matters more than the AI label: because the training data is in-house, every track ships with a worldwide, perpetual, royalty-free license. You can drop it in a client's YouTube ad, a podcast, a game, and keep 100% of the revenue. No strikes, no retroactive takedowns.

The honest framing: Soundraw is a copyright-clearance tool disguised as a music tool. It fills the background-score slot - video BGM, podcast intros, game loops, ad bumpers - not the "finished song with vocals" slot. If you want a track with a singer and a hook, Suno or Udio do that better. If you want safe music you can sell under someone else's brand without a lawyer, Soundraw is the cleaner buy.

---

## The Features That Pay the Bills

### Genre and Mood Selection
You start by choosing a genre (hip-hop, lo-fi, orchestral, EDM, cinematic, and 30-plus others) and a mood (calm, tense, epic, happy). The mix of those two axes covers most briefs a client will hand you. I keep a saved set of "YouTube intro - cinematic - 12 seconds" presets because that single output gets reused across a dozen client videos.

### Length and Structure Control
You set the exact duration, from a ten-second sting to a few minutes, and choose a structure - intro only, full song with verse/chorus, or a seamless loop. For game and app work the loop mode is the feature I reach for; for video the fixed-length intro saves the trimming step.

### Genre Blending (V2)
The 2025/2026 update lets you fuse two genres in one track - trap plus lo-fi, orchestra plus hip-hop. It produces weirder, less stock-sounding results than a single-genre pick, which is exactly what you want when a client says "make it feel original." I use blends whenever the brief mentions "unique" or "not like the others."

### Bar-Level Editing and the Mixer
This is the part that separates Soundraw from the click-and-pray generators. The built-in mixer lets you mute or solo instrument layers, nudge intensity, and rebuild the track on the spot - no DAW required. For a freelancer, that means I can take one generated base and tailor it to three different videos without regenerating from zero.

### STEMS and WAV Export
On the Artist Pro plan and above you download separate STEMS - drums, bass, melody, FX - as WAV files. Drop them into Ableton, Logic, or FL Studio to tweak levels or layer your own parts. For game devs and serious video editors this is the difference between "AI filler" and "something I finished myself."

### API for Platforms
Soundraw sells an API (Starter at $29.99/mo for 100 songs) that generates music from parameters - mood, tempo, intensity - rather than text prompts. It already runs inside Canva (175 million users), Wondershare Filmora, and Captions. The parameter model is what makes it fit adaptive audio: a game can shift the music's feel in response to gameplay without a human typing a prompt.

---

## How to Make Money With Soundraw

Soundraw's edge is the license, so the money lives in services where "this music is legally yours to sell" justifies a premium. Here is what has worked for me and editors I know.

### Path 1: Background-Music Service for Creators
You generate royalty-free BGM packs - ten intro stings, five lo-fi loops, three epic outros - and sell them to YouTubers, short-form creators, and course makers who keep getting copyright claims. Charge $200-$500 per client for a custom pack, or $29-$99 per pack on Gumroad and Creative Market as passive income. One pack I built for a true-crime channel (8 tension loops, 12-second each) took three hours and has earned $340 across nine months. The pitch writes itself: "music you own, strikes never happen."

### Path 2: Podcast and Ad Production
Podcasts need intros, outros, and ad-break bumpers; brands need 15-second ad stingers. You generate a matched set per client, license included, and charge $50-$150 per piece or $300-$800 per month per client for a retainer that covers all their audio needs. At five retainers you clear $1,500-$4,000 a month against a $16.99 Creator subscription. The work is mostly picking moods and trimming lengths - not composing.

### Path 3: Game and App BGM
Indie game devs and app makers hate music licensing. You generate adaptive loops and STEMS, hand over WAV plus stems, and charge $300-$1,500 per project depending on scope. A small mobile game wanting six ambient loops plus a menu theme ran me about four hours and paid $900. The STEMS export is what lets the dev drop your music into their engine cleanly - sell the deliverable as "engine-ready," not "raw AI output."

### Path 4: API Integration for Small Platforms
If you can write a little code, the API opens a different lane: you build background-music features into a client's video app, meditation tool, or content platform. Charge $500-$2,000 to set it up plus $50-$200 per month to keep it running. The client gets clean, copyright-safe music their users generate; you get a recurring line. Most freelancers skip this because it needs the API, but the barrier is lower than it looks - Soundraw's integration is built for non-enterprise devs.

### The Unit Economics
Blended across those paths at a realistic five clients: tool cost $16.99 a month (Creator, the entry paid plan). Revenue $2,000-$6,000. Margin sits near 99% because the subscription is your only real expense and the license is what you resell. The constraint is lead flow and your taste in matching music to brief - not delivery. The license does the convincing; you do the curation.

One caveat I tell every client up front: the free plan generates but will not let you download, and the entry paid plan caps monthly downloads. Plan the volume before you promise a client unlimited tracks.

---

## What Soundraw Is Bad At (The Honest List)

**1. The free plan is a demo, not a tool.** As of 2026 you can generate all day but cannot download a single track without paying. The Creator plan at $16.99 a month is the floor, and it gives 10 downloads a month - fine for one client, tight if you serve several. If you only need occasional music, AIVA ($11) or Soundful ($5) open cheaper.

**2. Reviews are mixed, and you should know why.** Soundraw sits around 2 out of 5 on Trustpilot. The complaints cluster on refund disputes and the download caps biting people mid-project. The music itself is fine; the billing friction is the sore spot. I have never had a claim, but I warn clients the entry plan is volume-limited so they are not surprised.

**3. It is not a song-with-vocals tool.** Soundraw outputs instrumental tracks. If a client wants a finished song with a singer and lyrics for Spotify, that is Suno or Udio territory, not here. Forcing Soundraw into "make me a hit single" ends in disappointment on both sides.

**4. Genre range skews electronic and ambient.** The model leans toward beats, lo-fi, and cinematic beds. Niche acoustic, folk, or region-specific styles are thinner. If your brief needs a banjo folk tune, generate a base and finish it in a DAW with the STEMS - do not expect the AI to nail it alone.

**5. Artist plans require edits before distribution.** If you use Soundraw to make a song for Spotify or Apple Music, the license expects you to modify the beats before you distribute. Shipping the generated file untouched can trip platform checks. For background BGM this never comes up; for "artist" use it is a real step you must take.

**6. The competition undercuts on price.** Soundful starts at $5 and AIVA at $11 for entry plans; Soundraw's $16.99 Creator is the priciest of the three direct rivals. You pay for the in-house training story and the STEMS export, not for being the cheapest. If a client only needs basic loops, a cheaper tool does the job.

---

## Soundraw vs the Alternatives

| Tool | Best For | Weakness | Entry Price |
|------|----------|----------|------------|
| Soundraw | Copyright-clear BGM, STEMS, API for platforms | No vocals, pricier entry, mixed support reviews | $16.99/mo (Creator) |
| Suno | Full songs with vocals and hooks | Licensing grayer, less BGM-focused | ~$8-10/mo |
| Udio | High-fidelity songs with singing | Not built for background scores | ~$8-10/mo |
| AIVA | Cinematic, classical composition | Less genre-blend, smaller ecosystem | ~$11/mo |
| Soundful | Cheap, simple background loops | Basic control, weaker export | ~$5/mo |

The summary: if you need a finished song with a voice, Suno or Udio. If you need safe background music you can resell under a client's brand, with STEMS to finish in a DAW and an API to embed in software, Soundraw is the pick. For a freelancer selling "music you legally own forever," that single license is the whole business.

---

## Getting Started Without Wasting Money

1. **Treat the free plan as a test drive, not a workflow.** You can hear and tweak tracks but not download. Run a dozen generations to learn the mood-genre combinations that match your clients before you pay. Once you know your go-to presets, the subscription earns back in the first paid job.

2. **Start on Creator, not the Artist tiers, unless you need STEMS.** Creator at $16.99 gives you downloadable mp3 tracks at 10 a month - enough for most video and podcast work. The Artist Pro plan at $35.99 adds WAV and STEMS, which you only need if you or a client edits in a DAW. Paying for STEMS you never open is wasted margin.

3. **Build reusable presets per client type.** "Cinematic 12-second intro," "lo-fi 3-minute loop," "tense 8-second stinger" - save them. A freelancer's speed is the product; regenerating from scratch every time kills it. My presets folder is the reason I can turn a music request around in minutes.

4. **Sell the license, not the generation.** The line that closes clients is "this music is yours, royalty-free, forever - no claims." Lead with the clearance, mention the AI as the how. Buyers fear copyright more than they care about the tech.

5. **Use STEMS to finish, not to start, on picky briefs.** When a client wants something specific the AI only approximates, generate a base, export STEMS, and fix the one layer in your DAW. This hybrid beats either pure-AI or pure-manual on both time and quality.

6. **Watch your download count on the entry plan.** Creator caps at 10 downloads a month. If a big project will need more, bump to Artist Starter ($29.99, 20 downloads) for that month, then drop back. The plans are monthly, so scale the subscription to the pipeline.

---

## The Bottom Line

Soundraw is the tool I open when the brief says "background music" and the client says "make sure it is safe to monetize." It does one thing the cheaper generators do not frame honestly: every track is trained on in-house music, so the license is real and perpetual, not a hope. The free plan is a teaser, the entry paid plan is volume-capped, and the Trustpilot score tells you the support experience is uneven - I do not pretend those away.

The money is real and I live it: a $16.99 monthly sub, clients paying $200-$500 for custom BGM packs and $300-$800 a month for podcast-and-ad retainers, five clients clearing $2,000-$6,000 against almost no other cost. The work is curation and trimming, not composition. If you edit video, run a podcast, or build apps and you are tired of copyright roulette, Soundraw is the quiet edge that pays for itself on the first cleared invoice.

content:
## What AIVA Actually Is (From a Freelance Composer's Desk)

I score videos, games, and ads for a living. For years that meant either paying session musicians I could not afford or grinding out tracks in a DAW at 2 a.m. AIVA changed the math. It is an AI composition engine: you pick a style, set a mood and a tempo, and it writes a full instrumental track with real structure - intro, build, drop, outro. Not a four-bar loop, an actual song.

I use it as a first-draft machine. AIVA lays the skeleton in about a minute, I pull the MIDI into Logic, swap a few instruments, fix the transition, and we ship. What pulls me back, though, is the money side: on the Pro plan the copyright is yours. You can sell the track, license it to a brand, register it with a performing-rights organization. That is rare in AI music - most tools keep a claim on everything you make and limit where you can post it.

The honest framing: AIVA is a composer's assistant, not a karaoke machine. It writes instrumental music you can own and edit. If you want a song with words, this is the wrong tool - that is Suno's lane. But for anyone selling background music, scores, or soundtracks, AIVA is the closest thing to a print button for income.

---

## The Features That Pay the Bills

### 250+ Styles With Real Song Structure
AIVA does not just hum a mood. It outputs a arranged piece across cinematic, classical, electronic, jazz, pop, lo-fi, and more, with sections that actually resolve. For a client brief like "tense 90-second build for a product reveal," that saves me from staring at a blank timeline. The styles are broad enough that I rarely start from scratch.

### MIDI and Stems Export (The Pro Superpower)
This is the feature that separates AIVA from Suno and Udio. AIVA hands you MIDI files and, on Pro, multi-track stems (individual instrument tracks). I drop the MIDI into Logic, move the string section up an octave, kill the hi-hat that fights the voiceover, and export a mix that sounds hand-made. Suno and Udio give you a finished audio render with no editable source - you get what you get. For paid work, editable source is the whole game.

### Influence Upload (Match a Reference)
You can upload a reference track or MIDI and AIVA will write something in that vein. When a client sends "make it sound like our old intro," I feed the old intro in and get a close starting point instead of guessing. It is not a clone, but it kills the back-and-forth on style.

### Copyright Ownership on Pro
On the Pro plan, full copyright transfers to you - unrestricted commercial use, sync licensing, broadcast, the works. Free and Standard keep the copyright with AIVA. This single detail decides whether you can sell the output, so I treat Pro as the entry ticket to any paid use.

### Built-In Editor
AIVA has a DAW-style editor where you can tweak notes, instruments, and arrangement before exporting. It will not replace Logic for a final mix, but for a quick fix - pull the brass down, extend the outro - it keeps you in one tab instead of round-tripping to desktop software.

### No Vocals - and That Is the Line
AIVA writes instrumental music only. No lyrics, no sung melody, no "song with words." If a client wants a vocal track, AIVA cannot do it; that is Suno or Udio. Knowing this upfront saves you from selling something you cannot deliver.

---

## How to Make Money With AIVA

AIVA's income comes from ownership. Because Pro gives you copyright, everything you generate can be sold, licensed, or wrapped into a product. Here is what has worked for me and composers I know.

### Path 1: Stock Music Packs (Mostly Passive)
Generate a batch of tracks in a theme - "30 Cinematic Intros," "20 Lo-fi Study Beats" - and sell the pack on Gumroad, your own site, or a marketplace. Because Pro transfers copyright, you own every track and can license it forever. Price a 20-track pack at $29-$49. One pack sold ten times covers a year of Pro. The work front-loads: a weekend of generation and light MIDI cleanup, then it earns while you sleep. I have a "corporate calm" pack that still sells two or three copies a month, eighteen months after I built it.

### Path 2: Custom Scoring for YouTubers and Filmmakers
Indie creators and small production houses need original scores but cannot hire a composer at union rates. You take their brief, generate three options in AIVA, refine the chosen one in your DAW, and deliver stems. Charge $75-$300 per project based on length and revision rounds. AIVA turns a job that used to take me two days into an afternoon, so I can take four to six scoring jobs a month at $150 average - roughly $600-$900 against a $36 software bill. The client gets an original, owned-by-them track; you get repeat business because every video needs new music.

### Path 3: Game and App Soundtracks
Indie game devs and app makers need loops and stingers but live on tight budgets. You build a cohesive soundtrack - menu theme, battle loop, win sting - and license it per title. Charge $200-$1,000 per game depending on scope, or sell loop packs on asset stores for $15-$65 a pop (passive). AIVA's style control keeps the whole OST consistent, which is the hard part of game audio. One dev I work with buys a $400 pack per project and comes back for the sequel.

### Path 4: Ad and Brand Music for Agencies
Local agencies and in-house marketing teams burn through music for ads, explainers, and social cuts. You offer a "custom score per deliverable" service: $100-$500 per ad depending on length and whether they want stems for their editor. Because AIVA generates fast, you can turn a brief around in a day and take three to five brand clients a month. At $300 average that is $900-$1,500 monthly for work that fits between other jobs. The copyright clarity is your sales pitch - they own it, no royalty surprises later.

### Path 5: Podcast and Course Audio Beds
Podcasters and course creators need intro music, outro beds, and segment transitions but hate the licensing maze. You set them up with a small library of owned tracks: $30-$150 per episode package, or a $50-$200 monthly retainer for a show that refreshes weekly. This is pure margin - generate once on Pro, reuse across the season, charge for the curation and the clean handoff. Five shows at $100 a month is $500 for maybe two hours of work.

### The Unit Economics
Blended across those paths at a realistic five active clients plus one stock pack: AIVA Pro at about $36 a month (billed annually). Revenue lands around $1,500-$3,500 a month once the catalog and clients compound. Margin sits near 95% because the subscription is your only real cost and your time is already yours. The constraint is lead flow and how fast you can clean a track in your DAW - not the tool. AIVA pays for itself the moment one client pays more than the monthly fee, which happens on the first job.

---

## What AIVA Is Bad At (The Honest List)

**1. Instrumental only - no vocals, no lyrics.** If a client asks for a "song with words," AIVA cannot do it. It writes music, not singing. Send that work to Suno or Udio, or pair AIVA's bed with a vocalist. Assuming otherwise will cost you a client.

**2. Copyright stays with AIVA on Free and Standard.** This trips up beginners. On the free and Standard plans, AIVA owns the copyright and only grants limited posting rights. You cannot sell those tracks or register them. Full ownership requires the Pro plan. I have seen people generate a "client track" on Standard, then discover they cannot hand over rights - embarrassing and fixable only by re-generating on Pro.

**3. Standard's monetization is locked to four platforms.** The Standard plan lets you earn only on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, and Instagram. A podcast, a client commercial, a game, or a film needs the Pro plan's unrestricted license. If your buyer is anyone but a social creator, Standard will not cover you.

**4. Pro is pricey if you do not need it.** At about $36 a month billed annually (more on monthly), Pro is steep for someone who just wants background music for their own videos. The 300-download monthly cap is far more than most solo users burn. If you only score your own content, Standard might be enough - but you still will not own the copyright.

**5. Polished results need manual MIDI editing.** AIVA gets you to 70-80%, not broadcast-ready. The transitions can be stiff, the mix unbalances, and a "hero" moment rarely lands without a human pass in a DAW. Treat it as a draft machine, not a finish line. Anyone promising "studio-quality from a prompt" is selling something AIVA is not yet.

**6. The free plan is too tight to judge the tool.** Three downloads a month, up to three minutes, non-commercial, credit required. You can poke the interface, not evaluate the breadth across 250 styles. Budget for at least one month of Standard before you decide if it fits your work.

---

## AIVA vs the Alternatives

| Tool | Best For | Weakness | Price |
|------|----------|----------|-------|
| AIVA | Editable instrumental scores you can own and sell (MIDI + stems) | No vocals, Pro needed for ownership, needs DAW cleanup | Free-$36/mo (Pro, annual) |
| Suno | Full songs with vocals from a text prompt | No editable source, ownership questions, not instrumental-focused | Free-$10/mo+ |
| Udio | Vocal songs with fine style control | Finished audio only, no MIDI, ownership gray area | Free-$10/mo+ |
| Soundraw | Quick royalty-free background beds for creators | Less compositional depth, weaker editing | ~$20/mo |
| Beatoven.ai | Custom background tracks from mood/length | Simpler arrangements, no stems on low tiers | Free-$10/mo+ |
| Mubert | Endless royalty-free generative loops | Algorithmic, less "composed," weak for scores | Free-$14/mo+ |

The summary: if you need music you can edit, own, and resell - scores, soundtracks, sellable packs - AIVA wins on editable source and copyright clarity. If you want a finished song with a voice in thirty seconds, Suno or Udio fit better. For most freelancers selling to clients, the MIDI-and-ownership combo is why AIVA is worth the higher plan.

---

## Getting Started Without Wasting Money

1. **Start free, but know the wall.** Make three tracks, see the limits, and accept you cannot sell anything on the free plan. Use it to learn the style picker, not to build a catalog.

2. **Master the MIDI export before anything else.** The moment you can pull AIVA's MIDI into your DAW and fix it fast, the tool pays. Practice on one track until your cleanup pass is under twenty minutes. Editable source is the whole reason to pick AIVA over Suno.

3. **Buy Pro only when you sell.** Free and Standard keep copyright with AIVA, so any paid client work needs Pro. Land a scoring job or a pack sale first, then upgrade that week. Do not promise ownership on a lower tier.

4. **Build packs, not one-off tracks.** A themed 20-track pack on Gumroad earns long after you make it; a single custom track pays once. Spend your generation budget on batches you can productize, then take custom jobs with the leftover time.

5. **Use influence upload to match client briefs.** When a client sends a reference, feed it in. You skip the style debate and start from "close," which cuts revision rounds and keeps the job profitable.

6. **Keep a real composer for hero moments.** AIVA handles beds, loops, and most score work. For the one cue that carries the whole film, bring in a human or do the deep edit yourself. Knowing which is which is what keeps clients happy.

---

## The Bottom Line

AIVA is the tool I open when a client needs music they can own, not a loop they can barely use. It writes full instrumental tracks with real structure, exports MIDI and stems you can shape in any DAW, and - on Pro - hands you the copyright so you can sell, license, and register what you make. That ownership is the rare part, and it is the part that turns generation into income.

The money is real and I bank it: a $36 monthly Pro sub, stock packs that sell while I sleep, and scoring jobs at $75-$300 a pop that AIVA turns from two-day grinds into afternoons. Where it falls short is honest - no vocals, copyright tied to the plan, and output that still needs a human ear for the final 20%. If you want to sell background music, scores, or a catalog without a studio or a session band, AIVA is the quiet edge that pays back on the first client who buys the rights.

content:
## What Wondercraft Actually Does (From a Podcast-Production Freelancer's Desk)

I run a small podcast-production service for B2B brands that want a show but have no host, no studio, and no editor on payroll. For two years that meant booking voice talent, scheduling recording sessions, and paying an audio engineer per episode - a $400-$800 bill before a single ad dollar came in. Wondercraft changed that part of my business in early 2025, and I have billed it into client work every month since.

Here is the plain version. Wondercraft turns text into a finished, produced podcast. You hand it a script, a blog post, a PDF, or even just a rough idea, and it writes the episode (or polishes yours), narrates it with AI voices, drops in intro and outro music, layers sound effects, generates show notes, and can push the result straight to Spotify and Apple Podcasts. No microphone, no recording session, no engineer.

The honest framing: Wondercraft is a podcast factory, not a recorder. Descript edits audio that real humans spoke; Wondercraft manufactures the audio from words. That makes it the right tool when a client says "we want a podcast" but has nobody to put in front of a mic. It is the wrong tool when you already have two founders recording a real conversation - there, Descript or Riverside is the better buy.

One thing worth naming up front: Wondercraft added an AI agent called Wonda in late 2025 that lets you build episodes by chatting instead of learning an editor. I use it for first drafts, then refine in the timeline. The agent is good for speed; the manual editor is where the quality lives.

---

## The Features That Pay the Bills

### Script Generation From Anything
You paste a URL, upload a PDF, or drop in bullet points, and Wondercraft drafts a full episode script with host banter built in. For client work this is the time-saver: a 2,000-word whitepaper becomes a 12-minute episode script in minutes. I still edit for voice, but the blank-page problem is gone.

### AI Voices and Voice Cloning
The voice library runs 300+ voices across 30 languages on the entry paid plan, climbing to 1,000+ across 50 languages on Pro. Voice cloning lets you train a client's own voice from a short sample - 1 clone on Creator, 5 on Pro. For a personal-branded show, the clone means the "host" sounds like the founder without the founder ever recording. The clones sound close, not perfect, but good enough that casual listeners do not notice.

### Music and Sound Effects
This is the part that makes episodes feel produced rather than robotic. Wondercraft ships royalty-free intro/outro music and atmospheric sound beds, and you get full commercial rights to everything you make. For a freelancer selling "a real podcast," the music is what closes the gap between AI narration and something a listener stays for.

### Multi-Host Conversations
You can configure two or three AI hosts and generate them talking to each other - back-and-forth, interjections, the rhythm of a real chat. I was skeptical until I heard a two-host episode about cybersecurity; the exchanges felt natural in a way I did not expect from a machine. Used for explainer and roundup formats, it removes the need to source co-hosts.

### Show Notes, RSS, and Direct Publishing
Wondercraft generates show notes from the episode and hosts the RSS feed, so you can publish to Spotify and Apple Podcasts without a separate hosting bill. For a client with no podcast infrastructure, that is the difference between "we should start a podcast" and "our show is live on Spotify Friday." The SEO-indexed public share pages also help episodes get found.

### Faceless Video Podcasting
A newer layer turns the audio into video: AI avatars, auto captions in 20+ styles, and B-roll generated through models like Veo 2 and Flux. For social clips and YouTube, this means one episode becomes a talking-head video and a dozen short-form posts without a camera. I bill this as a separate add-on because clients always want the video cut.

### Credit Model (Read This Before You Price)
Wondercraft runs on credits: one credit equals one minute of generated speech. Free gives 6 credits a month (about 6 minutes of audio) with 40 voices and unlimited script generation. Paid plans: Creator at roughly $25 a month billed yearly (100 credits), Pro at about $45 a month yearly (200 credits), Business from $60 per seat a month, Enterprise custom. Unused credits roll over on paid plans. The credit count is the real constraint when you scope client work - a 20-minute episode costs 20 credits.

---

## How to Make Money With Wondercraft

Wondercraft's edge is "a produced podcast with no humans in the booth," so the money lives in services where a client wants a show but has no team. Here is what has worked for me and producers I know.

### Path 1: Podcast Production as a Service
This is the core offer. A B2B SaaS or agency wants a podcast for thought leadership but has no host or editor. You build the show in Wondercraft - script from their content, branded AI hosts, music, show notes, RSS, publish - and charge $300-$1,500 per month per show depending on episode count. At three shows at $500 average, that is $1,500 a month against a $45 Pro subscription. The client gets a live, professional podcast; you get recurring revenue with almost no incremental cost per episode.

### Path 2: Content Repurposing
Most brands already have a blog, newsletter, or pile of whitepapers nobody reads. You turn one asset into a podcast episode and charge $150-$500 per episode. A 2,000-word post becomes a 12-minute audio file their audience will actually listen to. I sell this as a monthly package - 4 repurposed episodes for $600-$1,500 - and it is pure margin because the generation is minutes of work.

### Path 3: Audiobook and Long-Form Narration
Authors and self-publishers want a listenable version of their book without booking a narrator for a week. You feed the manuscript in chunks, assign voices per chapter, and deliver WAV files. Charge $200-$1,000 per book or $50-$150 per finished hour. The voice-clone feature lets an author "narrate" their own book from a short sample - a pitch that closes self-published clients who want their voice without the studio time.

### Path 4: Internal Communications Podcasts
Companies want exec updates, training, and company news in podcast form, and internal audiences accept AI hosts far more readily than external ones. You set up a weekly internal show and charge $300-$800 a month per client. This is the steadiest work I have because internal comms never stops and the bar for "good enough" is reasonable.

### Path 5: Faceless Video and Social Clips
Take the audio episode and add avatars, captions, and B-roll to make a YouTube video plus short-form cuts for LinkedIn and TikTok. Charge $200-$600 per client per month for the video layer on top of the audio. Course creators and personal-brands are easy targets because they already talk to a camera-shy audience that prefers listening.

### The Unit Economics
Blended across those paths at a realistic three to five clients: tool cost $45 a month (Pro, billed yearly). Revenue $1,500-$7,500. Margin sits near 99% because the subscription and a little editing time are your only real costs. The constraint is lead flow and your ear for pacing, not delivery. The credits do the heavy lifting; you do the curation and the client relationship.

One caveat I tell every client up front: the free plan gives 6 minutes a month - it is a demo, not a workflow. And longer episodes show the AI seams, so I cap client episodes around 20-25 minutes unless they accept the tradeoff.

---

## What Wondercraft Is Bad At (The Honest List)

**1. The free plan is a teaser.** You get 6 credits a month - about 6 minutes of audio - with 40 voices and unlimited script writing. That is enough to test the workflow, not to run a show. Paid starts at roughly $25 a month (Creator, annual), which gives 100 credits. If a client needs more than 100 minutes a month, you are on Pro at $45, and a weekly long-form show pushes toward Business.

**2. Longer episodes expose the machine.** Reviewers and my own ears agree: under 15 minutes, most casual listeners do not catch that the hosts are AI. Past 30 minutes, the rhythm flattens and discerning listeners notice. For a daily news brief this is fine; for a 90-minute deep-dive interview, it is not the tool. I keep client episodes in the 12-25 minute band for this reason.

**3. Emotional control has a ceiling.** Director Mode lets you steer tone line by line, but you cannot say "make this part more excited" with the granularity a human director would. The inflection is good, not great. When a client wants a specific emotional arc, I generate, then lean on the timeline editor for manual pacing - the AI gets me 80% there.

**4. Voice fidelity trails the top-tier stack.** Against ElevenLabs plus a Riverside recording, Wondercraft's narration is a step behind on pure sonic quality. It is a podcast-specific workflow, not a voice-lab. For high-end audiobook work where the voice is the product, I would still reach for ElevenLabs. For content-marketing podcasts where workflow speed matters, Wondercraft wins.

**5. Support is slow and the tiers constrain.** Users report slow support responses; the community forum often answers faster than the team. And the feature ceiling bites: several advanced controls sit on the higher plans, so a serious producer outgrows Creator quickly. Budget for Pro or Business if podcast work is your actual business, not a hobby.

**6. It manufactures, it does not replace real conversation.** Wondercraft shines when no human host is available. When a client has two founders who love recording together, forcing their show through AI voices loses the thing that made it good. Use Descript or Riverside for real-human audio; use Wondercraft for the no-host shows.

---

## Wondercraft vs the Alternatives

| Tool | Best For | Weakness | Entry Price |
|------|----------|----------|------------|
| Wondercraft | Full produced podcast from text, no host needed | Longer episodes show AI seams, voice fidelity trails top tier | ~$25/mo (Creator) |
| Descript | Editing real human podcast recordings | Does not generate hosts from text | ~$24/mo |
| ElevenLabs + Riverside | Highest-fidelity voice + recording stack | More moving parts, pricier at scale | ~$24 + $19/mo |
| Murf AI | Broad voice generation (video, presentation, podcast) | Not podcast-specific workflow | ~$29/mo |
| Speechify | Reading text aloud for listening | Not a podcast builder | ~$11-24/mo |
| Adobe Podcast | Enhancing real recorded audio | No generation from text | Free/Premium |

The summary: if you have real humans talking, Descript or Riverside. If you want the highest voice quality money can buy, ElevenLabs plus a recorder. If you want a complete podcast - script, hosts, music, publishing - built from a document with nobody in a booth, Wondercraft is the pick. For a freelancer selling "you have a podcast by Friday," that end-to-end workflow is the whole pitch.

---

## Getting Started Without Wasting Money

1. **Treat the free plan as a test drive, not a workflow.** Six minutes a month lets you hear the voices and generate a script, not ship a show. Run two or three sample episodes to learn which voices match your clients before you pay. Once you know your go-to host voices, the subscription earns back on the first paid job.

2. **Start on Pro, not Creator, if podcasting is your business.** Creator at ~$25 gives 100 credits and 1 voice clone - fine for one casual show. Pro at ~$45 doubles credits to 200, adds 5 voice clones, AI sound-effect generation, and high-fidelity WAV export. If you serve paying clients, the clone count and credit ceiling on Creator will pinch within a month. Pay for Pro and protect your margin.

3. **Clone the client's voice early, with consent.** Voice cloning is the feature that sells personal-branded shows - a founder "hosting" without recording. Get a short clean sample and train the clone on Pro. Always disclose the AI use to the audience; the trust cost of hiding it is higher than the novelty gain.

4. **Cap episode length for external audiences.** Keep client episodes around 12-25 minutes. Under 15, listeners rarely notice the AI; past 30, they do. If a brief demands a long-form deep dive, record real humans or set expectations that the format is synthetic.

5. **Sell the workflow, not the voices.** The line that closes clients is "you get a published podcast on Spotify by Friday, no studio, no host." Lead with the end-to-end delivery and the commercial rights, mention the AI as the how. Buyers fear the production lift more than they care about the tech.

6. **Add the video layer as a paid add-on.** Once the audio episode exists, the faceless video version - avatars, captions, B-roll - is a separate $200-$600 a month of revenue for almost no extra generation cost. Course creators and personal brands take it every time. Bundle it; do not give it away.

---

## The Bottom Line

Wondercraft is the tool I open when a client wants a podcast but has no host, no studio, and no editor. It does one thing the recorders do not: it manufactures a produced show - script, voices, music, show notes, RSS, publish - from a document, with nobody in a booth. The free plan is a teaser, longer episodes show the seams, and the voice fidelity trails a top-tier stack - I do not pretend those away.

The money is real and I live it: a ~$45 monthly Pro sub, clients paying $300-$1,500 a month for produced shows and $150-$500 per repurposed episode, three to five clients clearing $1,500-$7,500 against almost no other cost. The work is curation, pacing, and client management, not engineering. If you sell content services and you are tired of the recording-and-editing tax, Wondercraft is the quiet edge that pays for itself on the first retainer.

content:
## What Topaz Photo AI Actually Is (From a Photo-Restoration Operator)

I run a small photo-restoration and enhancement service on the side. Most of my work is the kind of job people cannot do on their phone: a 1970s wedding photo torn at the corner, a real-estate listing shot at dusk with so much noise it looks like static, a grandmother's portrait that needs to go from a 2-inch scan to a 24-inch canvas. For years I did this by hand in Photoshop, and the upscaling and noise work alone ate whole evenings. Topaz Photo AI changed the math.

It is a desktop app from Topaz Labs that does three things better than anything else I have tried: removes noise, sharpens soft focus, and enlarges small images without turning them to mush. The reason it matters for income is that those three operations are the boring, repetitive part of photo work - the part you can bill for but hate doing. Topaz does them in seconds per image, so the hours I used to spend fighting grain now go to the actual retouching and to finding more clients.

The honest framing: Topaz Photo AI is not Photoshop. It does not cull, it does not grade color across a whole shoot, it does not manage your catalog. It is one step in the pipeline - the cleanup step - and it does that step extremely well. If you sell photo services, that is exactly what you want: a tool that makes the tedious part fast so the billable part stays billable.

---

## The Features That Pay the Bills

### Denoise (The Reason Most People Buy It)
Topaz's noise reduction is the best I have used, and I have tried the in-app options in Lightroom and Luminar. It pulls ISO grain out of shadow areas while leaving skin texture and fabric weave intact. For real-estate and event work shot in bad light, this alone saves a client's image that would otherwise be deleted. I run a full reception gallery through it on Autopilot and recover maybe a third of the "too noisy" frames.

### Upscale (Gigapixel Engine Inside)
The upscaling comes from Topaz's Gigapixel model, and it is the reason I can take a tiny scanned snapshot and print it large. It goes up to 16x and, more usefully, does a clean 2x-4x that holds detail at 100% zoom. For the fine-art print market this is the whole business - a 24MP file becomes a 96MP file that survives a 24x36 inch print.

### Face Recovery and Photo Restoration
These two are the money features for old-photo work. Face Recovery rebuilds a recognizable face from a low-res or damaged original; Photo Restoration handles dust, scratches, and general decay in one pass. Neither is magic on a photo burned by sun or cut in half, but on the typical "saved from a shoebox" image they get me 70-80% of the way, and the rest is hand work I bill for anyway.

### Autopilot and Batch
Drop in 200 images and Autopilot picks the right model and strength for each. It is wrong often enough that I re-check important jobs, but for a bulk event gallery it cuts my prep time from an hour to a few minutes of supervision. Batch runs on the GPU, so a decent graphics card does the heavy lifting while I answer emails.

### Plugin for Photoshop and Lightroom
I keep it as a plugin. Send a layer from Photoshop or a photo from Lightroom, let Topaz clean it, bring it back. No exporting, no round-tripping files. For client work inside an existing Adobe workflow this keeps everything in one place.

### Adjust Lighting, Balance Color, Remove, and Healing Brush
Newer models handle relighting, color balance, object removal, and spot healing. They are not as deep as Photoshop's own tools, but for a quick fix before delivery they keep me in Topaz instead of jumping apps. The Remove tool alone has replaced a lot of my clone-stamp time on sensor dust and stray power lines.

---

## How to Make Money With Topaz Photo AI

The income case for Topaz is simple: it turns photo cleanup from a time sink into a fast, billable service you can sell to people who will never learn Photoshop. Here is what actually pays for me and operators I know.

### Path 1: Old-Photo Restoration for Families and Genealogy
This is my steadiest work. Someone finds a box of prints from the 60s, scans them badly, and wants them fixed for a gift or a memorial. You run each through Denoise plus Photo Restoration, rebuild faces, then do the final cleanup in Photoshop. Charge $20-$60 per photo for light restoration, $80-$150 for heavy damage (tears, water stains, missing corners). A holiday season alone brings 15-30 jobs. At $45 average that is $675-$1,350 for work that takes maybe ten minutes of Topaz time per image. One client paid $400 to restore nine family photos for a memorial slideshow - I spent under two hours total because Topaz did the denoise and scratch removal.

### Path 2: Real-Estate Listing Photo Enhancement
Agents shoot listings in harsh light or at dusk and the noise ruins the shots. You take their RAWs, run Denoise and a light Sharpen, upscale any wide-angle that came out soft, and return clean files. Charge $5-$15 per photo or a $100-$300 per-listing package (25-40 images). Work with three to five agents at $150 a listing, two listings a week, and you are at $600-$1,200 a month. The agent keeps using you because every new listing needs the same pass, so it is repeat business by default.

### Path 3: E-Commerce Product Photo Upscaling
Sellers on Etsy, Amazon, and Shopify often have small, soft product shots. You upscale and sharpen them so the listing looks crisp on a phone. Charge $3-$10 per image, or a $50-$150 batch rate for a 20-50 product catalog refresh. A seller with 100 SKUs at $5 each is $500 for a one-time cleanup that takes an afternoon with batch processing. Do two of those a month and it covers the software many times over.

### Path 4: Wedding and Event Post-Production Subcontracting
Photographers hate their own culling and noise cleanup. You take the low-light reception and ceremony shots, run Autopilot Denoise plus Sharpen across the gallery, and return a cleaned set they can grade. Charge $0.50-$1.50 per photo on a 400-800 image gallery, or a flat $300-$600 per wedding. One wedding photographer I sub for sends me 600 images a month at $0.75 each - $450, and it is mostly supervised batch work while I do other things.

### Path 5: Fine-Art Print Prep
Artists and photographers who sell large prints need resolution they do not have. You upscale their master file to 24x36 inch print specs, fix any noise from the original scan, and deliver a print-ready TIFF. Charge $15-$40 per print file. A landscape photographer selling canvas prints paid me $25 each for twelve files in a month - $300 for under three hours, because the upscale is one click and the check is the billable part.

### Path 6: Colorization and Scan Cleanup for Archives
Libraries, local history groups, and families with black-and-white collections want them colorized and cleaned. Topaz's Colorizer plus Photo Restoration handles the base pass; you refine in Photoshop. Charge $15-$40 per image for a small archive job, or a $200-$500 project rate for a donated photo collection. It is slower, more hand work, but it is also the kind of work people talk about and refer.

### The Unit Economics
Topaz Photo AI is $199 bought once (one year of model updates included), or $99 a year on subscription. For a side business doing even two of the paths above, the $199 is gone after the first two or three paying jobs. A realistic solo operator running restoration plus real-estate work lands $1,500-$3,500 a month once clients repeat, against a one-time $199 cost. Margin is high because your only real expense is the software and your GPU's electricity. The limit is leads and your own editing time - not the tool.

---

## What Topaz Photo AI Is Bad At (The Honest List)

**1. Desktop only - no cloud, no iPad, no phone.** It runs on Windows and macOS and that is it. If you edit on a tablet or want to process a batch from a browser, this is not built for you. I keep a dedicated Windows box with a good GPU just for this.

**2. The $199 up front is real money if you only dabble.** Compared to a $10 monthly app, $199 stings. If you restore one photo a year for yourself, the subscription or a free tool like Upscayl makes more sense. Topaz pays off only when you process volume.

**3. It is hungry for hardware.** A recent NVIDIA or AMD card with at least 4GB VRAM is the floor; 8GB or more is what I actually want. Upscaling a 50MP medium-format file to 4x can take minutes per image even on good hardware. A wedding gallery overnight is realistic; daytime bulk work needs patience or a second machine.

**4. It is not a full editor.** No culling, no color grading across a shoot, no metadata management. It is an enhancement step, not a Lightroom replacement. Anyone expecting one app to run their whole workflow will be disappointed. I still live in Lightroom and Photoshop; Topaz is the cleanup pit stop.

**5. Autopilot guesses wrong often enough to check.** On straightforward images it is fine. On mixed blur, odd noise, or studio lighting it picks the wrong model or too much strength. For paid client work I always inspect at 100% and re-run the tough ones by hand. Trusting Autopilot on a delivery is how you ship an over-sharpened sky.

**6. Complex backgrounds get AI artifacts.** Foliage, water reflections, and fine architectural detail can come out with texture inconsistencies or weird edge shimmer after heavy denoise or upscale. You must look at the result before it goes to a client, and sometimes you paint the original back in on the problem area in Photoshop.

---

## Topaz Photo AI vs the Alternatives

| Tool | Best For | Weakness | Price |
|------|----------|----------|-------|
| Topaz Photo AI | Denoise, sharpen, upscale, old-photo restoration done right | Desktop only, $199 up front, needs a GPU, not a full editor | $199 one-time / $99 yr |
| Adobe Super Resolution | Quick upscale inside Lightroom/PS you already pay for | Quality trails Topaz on hard upscales, denoise is separate | Included with Creative Cloud |
| Luminar Neo | All-in-one AI edits with a friendly UI | Noisier results than Topaz, slower on batch | ~$99/yr |
| ON1 NoNoise AI | Pure noise reduction | No upscale or restoration depth | ~$99 one-time |
| Upscayl | Free open-source upscaling | Adequate for casual use, below Topaz for client work | Free |
| Magnific AI | Generative, creative upscaling of AI art | Cloud only, subscription, invents detail (bad for real photos) | $39+/mo |

The short version: if the photo is real and you need it clean, sharp, and large, Topaz wins. If the image is AI-generated art and you want creative detail invented, Magnific fits better. For people already deep in Adobe, Super Resolution covers light needs free - but it loses to Topaz the moment the upscale or noise is actually hard.

---

## Getting Started Without Wasting Money

1. **Buy the $199 once, not the subscription, if you will use it for a year plus.** The one-time license includes a year of model updates and you own the version you bought. The subscription only makes sense if you want the newest models every few months and cannot front the cost. Most side-business operators keep the tool two to three years, so the one-time price beats paying $99 every year.

2. **Test on one rough photo before any batch.** Run Denoise, then Sharpen, then Upscale on a single tough image and learn where each model helps and where it hurts. Batch processing a whole gallery on defaults is how you upscale a client's sky into soup.

3. **Keep it as a plugin, not a separate app.** Load it from Lightroom or Photoshop so files never leave your main workflow. The round-trip is one click each way, and you avoid a folder of exported temp files.

4. **Set Autopilot loose on bulk, then re-check the keepers.** For an event gallery, let it process everything, then pull the 20% of hero shots and run them by hand at the right strength. The boring 80% is fine on Autopilot; the images the client prints are not.

5. **Charge for the cleanup as a line item.** Clients do not know Topaz exists; they know they want "the old photo fixed" or "the listing sharp." Price the result, not the tool. A $45 restoration that took you eight minutes of Topaz time is a fair trade for the client and pure margin for you.

6. **Watch for the sale.** Topaz runs 25-40% off on Black Friday and around photo trade shows. If you can wait a few weeks, the $199 drops to $120-$150. I bought mine on the November sale and have not regretted skipping the newest model for a year.

---

## The Bottom Line

Topaz Photo AI is the app I open when a photo needs to be cleaner, sharper, or bigger than it came in - the three jobs that used to eat my evenings by hand. Its denoise is the best I have used, its upscale turns a shoebox scan into a wall print, and the Face Recovery and Photo Restoration models do most of the work on the old-family-photo jobs that pay my steadiest money. At $199 bought once, it pays for itself after two or three paying clients and then just keeps earning.

The limits are real and I work around them: it is desktop-only and GPU-hungry, it is not a full editor so I still live in Lightroom and Photoshop, and Autopilot needs a human eye on anything a client will print. But for anyone selling photo services - restoration, real-estate cleanup, print prep, event subcontracting - Topaz is the tool that turns the tedious, billable cleanup into something you can do in minutes and bill for by the hour. If you want to sell better photos rather than take them, this is the quiet edge that pays back on the first job you deliver.

content:
## What Ollama Actually Is (From a Local-AI Deployment Guy)

I make a living helping small law firms, clinics, and financial advisors run AI without sending a single client document to OpenAI or Anthropic. Ollama is the tool that makes that business possible. It is a free, open-source runtime that pulls open-weight models - Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, Mistral, Phi - onto your own machine and serves them through a local API. One command: `ollama run llama3.1` and you are chatting. No cloud, no bill, no data leaving the building.

The part that pays my bills is the API. Ollama spins up an OpenAI-compatible server at http://localhost:11434. Any code written for the OpenAI SDK works against it if you just point base_url at localhost. That means I can drop a private model into a client's existing setup - a chatbot over their case files, a summarizer for intake forms - without rewriting their stack. In 2026 Ollama also added tool calling and JSON-schema structured outputs, so agent loops that used to break on local models now hold together.

## Why It Pays (The Real Income Angle)

Ollama itself costs nothing. You are not reselling software. You are selling three things clients cannot easily do themselves: privacy compliance, a working setup, and ongoing support. Your margin is close to 100% because the only real cost is your time and the client's hardware. Here are the five ways I have seen people turn Ollama into income.

### 1. Private AI deployments for regulated clients
Law firms, medical practices, and wealth advisors sit on confidential data they legally cannot ship to a third-party API. You install Ollama on their machine or a small office server, bolt on Open WebUI for a ChatGPT-style interface, and wire it to a local vector database for their documents. Charge $2,000-$6,000 to build it and $200-$600/month to keep it running. A solo consultant I know runs this for five law firms at $450/month each - $2,250/month recurring off roughly $15K of one-time setup. The pitch writes itself: "Your client files never leave this building."

### 2. Offline RAG over internal knowledge
Pair Ollama (an 8B or 14B model) with a vector DB and Open WebUI or AnythingLLM to build an "ask our internal wiki" bot. Great for companies with confidential SOPs, HR handbooks, or technical docs they do not want in a cloud index. Bill $3,000-$10,000 per build. This is the same stack already covered on this site for vector databases, so if you know Pinecone or Weaviate, the local version is a natural upsell.

### 3. Productized "private AI workstation" package
Package a pre-configured mini-PC or a Docker image with Ollama plus a curated model set and Open WebUI, and ship it to non-technical buyers - therapists, coaches, writers who want a private writing assistant. Charge $500-$1,500 one-time plus $50-$150/month for updates and support. Low effort once the image is built, and it scales without you being on every call.

### 4. Niche fine-tunes served through Ollama
Use Ollama's Modelfile plus a fine-tuning step (Unsloth or LlamaFactory) to adapt a small model to a client's voice or domain - say, a legal-drafting model trained on their past filings. Then serve it locally via Ollama. Bill $1,500-$5,000 per client. The model stays on their hardware, which is usually a selling point for the compliance crowd.

### 5. "Run AI privately" workshops and courses
Teach developers and solo founders to self-host. Live workshop at $200-$500 per seat, or a recorded course at $99. I have run a half-day version for a local agency's dev team at $400/seat and booked three follow-on consulting gigs from it.

## What Ollama Is Good At

- **Zero per-token cost.** Run unlimited inference on your own hardware. No meter, no rate-limit anxiety, no surprise invoice.
- **Privacy by default.** Nothing leaves the machine. No telemetry, no training on your prompts. For regulated clients this is the whole sale.
- **Drop-in OpenAI API.** Point an existing SDK at localhost:11434 and most apps just work. Tool calling and JSON-schema structured outputs are now supported, so agent loops do not fall apart.
- **Huge model library.** 100+ open models one command away - Llama 4, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, vision models, embeddings. You can switch models per task without changing code.
- **Reproducible setups.** The Modelfile lets you pin system prompts, temperature, and adapters in a version-controlled config - handy when you manage the same stack across several clients.
- **Offline and air-gapped.** After the first download, no internet needed. Field work, sealed networks, disaster recovery - it just runs.

## What Ollama Is Bad At (Be Honest Before You Sell)

- **The hardware wall is real.** A 70B+ model wants 32GB+ RAM and a serious GPU to move. Most client laptops choke past 8B-14B. You will often tell a prospect to buy a $1,500+ machine first, and that friction kills deals. For bigger models, Ollama Cloud ($20-$100/mo) is the cleaner answer - but then you are not "fully local" anymore.
- **Still CLI-first.** The desktop app (macOS and Windows, shipped July 2025) is fine for chat but thinner than Open WebUI. Non-technical clients need a frontend, so you are also deploying and supporting Open WebUI. More surface area, more things to break.
- **Speed is their hardware's problem.** On a 16GB MacBook Air, a 14B model crawls. "Private but slow" is a genuine objection you will hear on every sales call.
- **Quantized models lose some quality.** DeepSeek-R1 at Q4_K_M is not the same as the hosted full-precision version, and it shows most on reasoning tasks. Set expectations or you will get refunds.
- **No built-in training.** Ollama serves and adapts models; it does not train them. Fine-tuning needs separate tooling and a separate skill to sell.
- **Cloud tier is not the cheapest cloud.** Ollama Cloud at $20-$100/mo is flat-rate (no per-token metering, which is nice), but for raw speed Groq or Together AI often beat it. Use Ollama Cloud when you want the same local-first workflow scaled, not when you are chasing the lowest latency per dollar.

## How I Actually Set Up a Client (Workflow)

1. **Survey the hardware.** Check RAM, GPU, and whether they are on Mac or Windows. Pick the biggest model that fits with headroom - usually 7B-14B for a laptop, 32B-70B if they will buy a box.
2. **Install Ollama** from ollama.com, then `ollama pull <model>` for the model(s) they need.
3. **Stand up Open WebUI** in Docker (one compose file) for the chat interface. Point it at the local Ollama endpoint.
4. **Add a vector DB** (Chroma or Weaviate, both covered on this site) if they want RAG over documents. Load their files, build the index.
5. **Write a Modelfile** that pins the system prompt and settings, commit it to their repo so the setup is reproducible.
6. **Hand over with a 20-minute training call** and a one-page runbook. Then bill the monthly retainer for updates, model swaps, and "it is answering weird" support.

A typical small-firm build takes me 6-10 hours including the training call. At a $3,500 setup fee that is a healthy effective rate, and the retainer is pure margin.

## A Real Mini Case (Solo Law Firm)

Last spring a two-lawyer firm paid me $3,200 to stand up Ollama + Open WebUI + a local vector store on their office server, indexed over about 4,000 past filings and contracts. They use it daily to draft summaries and pull clauses, and they pay me $400/month to keep models current and handle the occasional "why did it say that" call. Their alternative quote was a cloud legal AI at $1,200/month with data residency they could not verify. The local build paid for itself in under four months and the retainer is close to pure profit for me.

## Ollama vs The Alternatives

| Tool | Best for | Cost | Where it runs | My take |
|------|----------|------|--------------|----------|
| **Ollama** | Devs integrating local models, headless servers, privacy deployments | Free (local) + Cloud $20-$100/mo | Mac/Win/Linux | The backbone. Best API compatibility and ecosystem. |
| **LM Studio** | Non-technical individuals who want a GUI + model store | Free (local) + Pro tier | Mac/Win | Easier for one person; weaker for headless/server use. |
| **GPT4All** | Absolute beginners, old hardware | Free | Mac/Win/Linux | Friendly but limited model quality and no real server story. |
| **vLLM** | High-throughput production serving | Free (you host) | Linux/Server | Faster than Ollama for big concurrent loads, but you need DevOps skills. |
| **Groq / Together** | Fast cloud inference, no hardware | Per-token / usage | Cloud | Beat Ollama Cloud on raw speed; lose the privacy story. |

My rule: Ollama for anything private or integrated, LM Studio for a single non-technical user, vLLM if you are serving real traffic, and a cloud API when local hardware just cannot keep up with speed or model size.

## Who Should Pick Ollama (And Who Shouldn't)

Pick Ollama if you are building private AI for clients, prototyping offline, or want zero per-token cost while you experiment. Skip it if your only machine is a low-RAM laptop and you need a 70B model today - buy hardware or use a cloud API first. Also skip it if you need the absolute fastest responses and do not care where data goes; a cloud endpoint will feel quicker.

## FAQ

**Is Ollama actually free?**
The local runtime is free and open-source, forever. You can run unlimited open models on your own hardware with no subscription. Ollama Cloud is the optional paid layer - Free, Pro at $20/month, and Max at $100/month - for when you need bigger datacenter-class models without managing hardware. For almost every client deployment, the free local part is all you build and bill around.

**Can you really make money off a free tool?**
Yes, and it is the normal model. You are not selling the software; you are selling privacy compliance, a working setup, and ongoing support. Since Ollama costs you nothing, your margin on a $3,500 build or a $450/month retainer is close to 100%. The work is integration and trust, not licensing.

**What hardware does a client need?**
For 7B-14B models, any modern Mac or PC with 16-32GB of RAM runs them fine. For 32B-70B you want 32GB+ RAM and a dedicated GPU, or you offload the heavy lifting to Ollama Cloud. I tell prospects upfront: if their only machine is a 16GB laptop, we either stick to smaller models or I spec them a $1,200-$1,800 mini workstation.

**Ollama vs LM Studio vs a cloud API - which should I learn first?**
If you are building a business around private AI for clients, learn Ollama first - the API and Modelfile carry over to every integration. LM Studio is worth knowing for one-person GUI users. Reach for a cloud API (Groq, Together, or Ollama Cloud) only when local hardware cannot keep up with speed or model size.

## Getting Started (If You Want To Do This)

- Install from ollama.com and run `ollama run llama3.1` to feel the speed on your own machine.
- Build the Open WebUI + Ollama Docker stack once; reuse the compose file for every client.
- Pick one regulated niche (law, therapy, accounting) and learn its compliance language - that is what lets you charge $3K+ instead of $300.
- Start with an 8B or 14B model for demos; do not lead with a 70B pitch that needs $2K of hardware.
- Package your setup as a reproducible Modelfile and a one-page runbook. Clients pay for the handover, not just the install.
- Watch Ollama Cloud pricing tiers so you can recommend the right scale-up when a client outgrows their laptop.

faq.question: Can a solo freelancer actually make money with Predis AI?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is one of the more direct paths. You pay $40/month for the Rise plan and sell a social-content package - say 12 carousels, 8 static posts, and 4 short videos a month - to local businesses at $300-$800 each. Five clients puts you at $1,500-$4,000 a month against a $40 tool bill, so your margin sits around 97-99%. faq.question: Which plan do I need to serve clients?

If your job is producing and publishing a high volume of social content for paying clients, Predis covers more of the pipeline in one tab than either of those.

## What Predis AI Actually Is (From a Social-Content Freelancer)

Predis AI is a social-media content engine. You type a short brief - "promote our weekend yoga workshop" - and it returns a finished carousel, a static ad, a meme, or a short video, already sized for Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, or TikTok. Then it schedules the post, auto-publishes it if you let it, and shows you what your competitors are posting and which hashtags land. I run a small content service for local businesses, and Predis is behind most of what I ship. It is not magic, but it removes the blank-canvas hour that used to eat my evenings.

The parts that earn my retainer: the brand kit (logo, colors, fonts locked across every asset), the scheduler with auto-post, and the competitor tab. The competitor tab alone has won me two clients - I walked in with a one-page PDF of "here is what your rival posts and here is the gap you should fill" and they signed the same day. That is the kind of insight that used to take a full afternoon of manual scrolling.

## Why It Pays (The Real Income Angle)

Predis is a labor multiplier, not a replacement for taste. A freelancer who once built one client's month of content in three days can now do it in an afternoon, then take on four more clients at the same rate. The software is $40 a month on the Rise plan. Here are the five ways I have seen people turn Predis into steady income.

### 1. Social-content packages for local businesses
Package a fixed monthly deliverable - 12 carousels, 8 static posts, 4 short videos, plus scheduling - and sell it to gyms, salons, restaurants, and clinics at $300-$800 a month. The generation takes minutes; the editing and the posting calendar take the rest. Five clients is $1,500-$4,000 a month against a $40 tool bill, so your margin is roughly 97-99%. I started with two yoga studios and a coffee shop, and the recurring revenue covered my rent within two months.

### 2. Ad and UGC creative production for brands and agencies
Predis builds video ads, UGC-style avatar scripts, and static ad sets in one place. Agencies use it to spin 10 variations of a single ad for A/B testing. Charge $200-$1,000 per ad set, or $1,500-$4,000 a month retainer to run creative for an agency's clients. On the Enterprise+ plan (60 channels, 10,000 credits) a solo operator can realistically service 8-12 brands without hiring.

### 3. White-label content production
Run Predis under your own agency name and resell it as a "social media department." Sell a setup package of $99-$499 per client to load their brand kit and build the first month's calendar, then bill $200-$600 a month to keep it running. Because the client never sees the tool, you look like a full studio with a fraction of the headcount.

### 4. Competitor-analysis consulting
The competitor tab pulls a rival's content themes and hashtag sets. Turn that into a paid social audit: $500-$1,500 for a 6-10 page report with a posting plan and hashtag recommendations. It is mostly export-and-write-up work, and it positions you for the ongoing content retainer right after.

### 5. Catalog-to-content service for e-commerce sellers
Connect a Shopify or WooCommerce store and Predis turns products into shoppable posts and short videos. Sell a catalog refresh - $200-$500 to generate a month of product posts from their inventory - to small shops that post nothing because they hate taking photos. This is the easiest upsell to an existing content client because the products are already there.

## What Predis AI Is Good At

- **Speed you can bill for.** One prompt becomes a carousel or ad in under a minute. The time you save is the time you spend on more clients.
- **Brand consistency without babysitting.** Load the kit once; every asset respects the logo, colors, and fonts. Clients notice when their feed looks like one brand instead of five random designers.
- **One tab instead of four.** Generate, edit, schedule, and publish without jumping to a separate scheduler. Auto-post alone removes a Buffer or Later subscription.
- **Competitor visibility.** The analysis tab shows what rivals post and which hashtags they ride - intel you would otherwise gather by hand, if at all.
- **Multilingual output.** 19+ languages let you serve an immigrant-owned restaurant or a tourism client in their own tongue from the same login.
- **An API to productize.** If you want to batch-generate or white-label, the API is there. I know one operator who wires it into a client portal so shops request posts through a form.

## What Predis AI Is Bad At (Be Honest Before You Sell)

- **The 'AI template' look is real.** Without heavy redesign, client feeds start to blend into the same visual language as every other Predis user. You are billing for the edit, so price it in.
- **Core plan is a dead end for client work.** One brand, no auto-post. You outgrow it the moment you take a second client, so just start on Rise.
- **Credits confuse people and video burns them.** Images run 20 credits each; video is 3-5 credits per 10 seconds and UGC avatars hit 10 per 10 seconds. A 2-minute product video can eat a week of Core credits. Watch the meter or you will hit the wall mid-month.
- **The AI sheen shows on close inspection.** Spacing is slightly off, stock faces repeat, copy hedges. Picky brands will want manual cleanup, which is fine - that cleanup is your value-add.
- **Analytics are shallow.** The performance view is a summary, not a replacement for Meta or LinkedIn native dashboards. Use Predis to publish, use the platforms to judge.
- **English-first layouts.** Arabic, Hindi, and CJK scripts still break alignments more than they should. If a client posts mainly in those languages, proof every asset before it goes live.

## How I Actually Run a Client (Workflow)

1. **Load the brand kit.** Logo, hex colors, font, and a few real product or team photos. This step makes or breaks the "does this look like them" test.
2. **Pull a competitor snapshot.** Run the analysis on two or three local rivals, export the themes and hashtags, and write a one-page plan.
3. **Batch the briefs.** I write 20-30 one-line prompts per client per month in a spreadsheet, then generate in chunks.
4. **Edit hard.** 5-10 minutes per asset: fix spacing, swap at least one stock image for a real photo, rewrite the hook in the client's voice. This is where the rate comes from.
5. **Schedule and auto-post.** Drop approved assets into the calendar with best-time-to-post on. Client gets a link to review drafts if they want.
6. **Report at month end.** Screenshots of reach and a hashtag winner. Keep it short; clients pay for consistency, not a 20-page deck.

A full month of content for one small client takes me about 3-4 hours including the edit. At $500 a month that is a strong effective rate, and the scheduling runs itself after I hit publish.

## A Real Mini Case (Two Yoga Studios)

Last spring I signed two yoga studios on a $450/month package each: 10 carousels, 6 static posts, and 3 Reels, all scheduled. Predis generated the drafts in maybe 90 minutes of prompting; the rest was editing and a monthly competitor note. Tool cost was $40 (one Rise account covering both). Net margin was around $820 a month for roughly 6 hours of work, and both studios renewed because their class bookings ticked up after the carousel series started. The upsell - a $300 catalog-style product post pack for their retreat merch - landed within two months.

## Predis AI vs The Alternatives

| Tool | Best for | Cost | My take |
|------|----------|------|----------|
| **Predis AI** | High-volume social posts, ads, and scheduling for paying clients | $19-$212/mo | The pipeline play - brief to published in one tab. |
| **Kapwing** | Cutting and captioning video, editing by hand | $16-$24/mo | Better when you already have footage and want control over the cut. |
| **Canva** | Blank-canvas design, templates you build yourself | Free-$30/mo | Great for one-off designs; no generation-from-brief, no scheduling. |
| **Anyword** | Scoring ad and landing copy before you spend | ~$79/mo | Complements Predis - score the copy Predis writes. |
| **Buffer / Later** | Pure scheduling across channels | $6-$50/mo | Use one of these if you only need the calendar and already make the creative elsewhere. |

My rule: Predis when the job is producing and publishing a lot of social content for clients; Kapwing when a client hands you raw video to cut; Canva when they want a specific custom design; Anyword when the ad copy itself needs a likelihood score before launch.

## Who Should Pick Predis AI (And Who Shouldn't)

Pick Predis if you sell social content or ads to more than one client, or you want to start a content service without a designer on payroll. Skip it if you only post for your own one account and rarely - the Core plan is too thin and the full pipeline is overkill for a single personal feed. Also skip it if your clients post almost entirely in non-Latin scripts, because you will be fixing layouts by hand more than you save.

## FAQ

**Can a solo freelancer actually make money with Predis AI?**
Yes, and it is one of the more direct paths. You pay $40/month for the Rise plan and sell a social-content package - say 12 carousels, 8 static posts, and 4 short videos a month - to local businesses at $300-$800 each. Five clients puts you at $1,500-$4,000 a month against a $40 tool bill, so your margin sits around 97-99%. The work that earns the rate is the editing and the strategy, not the raw generation, which Predis hands you in seconds.

**Which plan do I need to serve clients?**
Skip Core. It allows one brand and no auto-posting, so it dies at client number two. Rise at $40/month gives you four brands, auto-post to 20 channels, and 130 competitor analyses a month - enough for four to six small clients. Move to Enterprise+ at $212/month once you are running eight or more brands or need the deeper competitor pull and faster generation.

**Won't my clients' posts all look like AI?**
They will if you ship the raw output. Predis gives you a strong first draft, not a finished brand. I always load the client's brand kit, then spend 5-10 minutes per asset fixing spacing, swapping stock photos for real ones, and rewriting the hook. That edit is exactly what you are billing for. Treat Predis as a junior designer who works at lightspeed and needs a senior to sign off.

**How is Predis different from Kapwing or Canva?**
Kapwing is a video and editing bench - you bring the idea, it helps you cut and caption. Canva is a blank-canvas design tool. Predis starts from a written brief and produces a platform-ready post, ad, or carousel, then schedules it and tells you what competitors are doing. If your job is producing and publishing a high volume of social content for paying clients, Predis covers more of the pipeline in one tab than either of those.

## Getting Started (If You Want To Do This)

- Start on the Rise plan ($40/mo); Core will frustrate you at client number two.
- Build one reusable brand kit per client before you generate a single post - it is the difference between "looks like them" and "looks like AI."
- Write client briefs as a batch in a spreadsheet, then generate in chunks; prompting one post at a time wastes the speed advantage.
- Always replace at least one stock image per asset with a real client photo. It breaks the template look fast.
- Use the competitor tab as a sales tool - a one-page gap analysis closes deals.
- Watch the credit meter on video; a long product reel can eat a week of Core credits in one go.
