content:
## What Patreon Actually Is (From a Creator Who's Run a Page)

I've run a Patreon page for a couple of years - first to fund a writing newsletter, later to host an AI-tools community with paid tiers. So this comes from the creator side, not Patreon's sales deck. Patreon is a membership billing system. You set up tiers - say $5 for behind-the-scenes posts, $15 for a private Discord and monthly assets - and people who like your work subscribe and get charged every month automatically. Patreon takes a cut, processes the cards, handles tax for foreign fans, and drops the rest in your account. That's the deal: you bring the audience, they handle the plumbing.

The part that works is the recurring charge. A one-time sale asks the customer to decide again next time. A Patreon pledge just renews. For a creator with a real following, that auto-renew is the difference between scrambling for each sale and having a baseline income you can plan around.

## How People Actually Make Money On It

Patreon is a billing layer, not a crowd. The money comes from what sits behind the tiers:

1. **Paid communities.** This is the big one in 2026. Bundle a private Discord, a monthly live call, and a resource library, charge $10-25, and you've got recurring income that one-time product sales can't match. Whop (covered on this site) does gated communities too, but Patreon's brand is what fans already recognize.
2. **Exclusive content and newsletters.** Writers and artists put patron-only posts, early drops, or a members-only email behind a tier. Low production cost, high perceived value.
3. **AI-generated asset memberships.** A clean angle: every month you drop a fresh pack of prompts, templates, or workflow docs your patrons can use. Near-zero marginal cost, which is exactly why it pairs well with the AI tools reviewed elsewhere here.
4. **Tutorial and coaching tiers.** Charge more for a monthly group call or a review of the patron's work. The higher tier subsidizes the lower one.

Reality check on the numbers: 100 patrons at $10 a month is $1,000 gross. After Patreon's 10% and card processing, you keep roughly $840. At 500 patrons you're clearing about $4,200 a month - real money from a loyal audience, with no inventory and no ad spend. The catch is the audience has to already exist. Patreon's own data and every creator I know confirms it: pages built by someone with zero following make almost nothing, because the platform sends them almost no traffic.

## What It Really Costs

There is no monthly fee to open a page. You pay a percentage of what you collect. For pages created after Patreon's 2025 pricing change, that's a flat 10% platform cut. Older pages sit on legacy plans ranging from 5% to 12% depending on the tier (Lite, Pro, Premium). On top of that comes payment processing of about 2.9% plus $0.30 per charge.

Two things bite:

- **The stack adds up.** On a $10 pledge: 10% is $1.00, processing is about $0.59, so you keep roughly $8.41. Call it 16% total taken on a typical charge. The legacy 12% Premium plan pushes that higher than any other major creator platform.
- **Sub-$3 tiers get punished.** Pledges under $3 switch to a micro-transaction rate of about 5% plus $0.10. A $1 tier nets you around $0.75 after everything. Most creators set their lowest tier at $3 or more just to dodge that.

Payouts land monthly, usually around the 5th, after a short hold for new creators. Patreon also collects and remits VAT for international patrons, which is genuinely useful - you don't file that paperwork yourself - though it can nudge EU fans toward cheaper tiers.

## Where It Falls Short

- **You don't own the relationship.** Patreon can change fee terms, freeze payouts during a dispute, or enforce content rules that affect your niche. A policy shift or a frozen account can cut your income with little warning. Smart creators treat Patreon as one rail, not the whole train.
- **Discovery is weak.** There's an Explore page, but almost nobody browses Patreon to find new creators. You will bring 100% of your own traffic from YouTube, a newsletter, or social. If you were hoping Patreon would hand you an audience, it won't.
- **No built-in email marketing.** You can export your patron list, but Patreon won't nurture them for you. Churn tools and deeper analytics sit behind paid legacy tiers.
- **Content rules are strict.** No adult content, and AI-generated material has to follow their policies. If your monetization depends on edgy or borderline content, read the terms first.
- **The 10% stings at scale.** Once you're past a few thousand a month, that flat cut is real money. At $5,000 monthly gross you hand Patreon about $500 plus processing - at which point a self-run Stripe stack starts looking cheap.

## Patreon vs The Field

| If you want to... | Best pick | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recurring monthly income from fans | Patreon | Auto-charging tiers, brand trust |
| Run a gated community / Discord | Whop | Built-in access gating |
| Sell a one-time file or template | Gumroad | Zero monthly cost, live in minutes |
| Take tips with near-zero fees | Ko-fi | 0% platform fee on free plan |
| Own the stack at high volume | Your own Stripe | No platform percentage |

## Getting Started

1. Sign up and name your page - a few minutes, no card required.
2. Set 2-3 tiers with clear perks. Start your lowest at $3+ to avoid the micro-processing penalty.
3. Wire up patron-only posts or a Discord so paying members get something the day they join.
4. Put your Patreon link where your audience already is - video descriptions, a newsletter sign-off, your social bio.
5. Watch the first payout around the 5th; expect a short hold while Patreon checks for failed cards.

## The Honest Bottom Line

Patreon is the most recognized name in creator memberships, and for good reason - the recurring billing, tax handling, and brand trust save you from building that machinery yourself. For a creator with an audience, it turns attention into a predictable monthly income better than any one-off product. The mistake is treating it as a growth engine. It is a checkout for people who already like you; it will not find them. Launch here to capture the fans you have, keep your lowest tier at $3 or above, and once you're past a few thousand a month, run the math on a self-run Stripe setup before Patreon's 10% becomes the biggest line item in your business.

faq.question: Can you actually make money on Substack, or is it only for famous writers?

As of early 2026 Substack reports about 8.4 million paid subscriptions and over 17,000 writers earning, so the model pays real people. faq.question: Do I own my audience, and can I leave if I outgrow it?

The limit: app-only readers and Notes followers do not fully transfer if you move. content:
## What Substack Actually Is (From Someone Who's Run a Paid Newsletter)

I've published on Substack for a few years - started free to build a readership, then flipped a slice of it to paid. So this is written from the operator's chair, not Substack's marketing copy. Substack is a newsletter platform with billing bolted on. You write posts, they go out by email and also live on your Substack page, and you can put a paywall in front of some of them. Readers pay monthly or yearly; Substack collects the money, sends the emails, and pays you after taking its cut. That's the whole pitch: write, and the rest is handled.

The part that pulled me in is the zero-risk start. There is no monthly fee, no subscriber cap, no feature gate. You can run a free newsletter to 50,000 readers and pay nothing. Only when someone pays do you part with money - 10% of that subscription, plus Stripe's processing of about 2.9% and $0.30 per charge. On a $10 subscriber you keep roughly $8.41. The 10% never drops, no matter how big you get.

## How People Actually Make Money On It

Substack is a publishing-and-billing tool, not a crowd. The income comes from the audience you bring and the wall you put up:

1. **Paid newsletters around a niche.** This is the core play. Pick a topic people will pay to follow - AI tool breakdowns, market commentary, a trade newsletter - and charge $5-15/month. A writer with 2,000 free readers and a 5% paid conversion has 100 paying subs at $8 = $800/month, before scaling. The recommendation network (more on that below) is what makes cold starts possible.
2. **Founding-member and annual tiers.** Offer a $100-250 founding tier for superfans and push annual billing. Annual cuts Stripe's $0.30 fee from 12 charges to 1, so each annual sub nets you a few dollars more - and annual readers churn less.
3. **Bundle audio and video.** Substack hosts podcasts and video posts under the same paywall. Creators add a paid podcast feed or weekly video without a second platform. It will not replace a real podcast host, but for a writer adding audio as a bonus it is free and good enough.
4. **Chat community as a paid perk.** Paid subscribers get a Substack Chat space - threaded discussion, basically a light Discord. Bundle it with the newsletter at $15-25 and you get recurring income that one-time product sales (covered on this site under Gumroad) cannot match.

## The Recommendation Network Is the Real Growth Engine

Most platforms leave you to find readers yourself. Substack does not. Its recommendation system cross-promotes publications: when a reader subscribes to a writer you recommend, they are nudged to subscribe to you too. For a lot of newsletters this drives 30-50% of new signups, and it costs nothing. Notes - Substack's short-post feed, like a quieter Twitter - pulls people back to your full posts. I have watched a brand-new publication hit its first 100 paid readers almost entirely through recommendations and Notes, with zero ad spend. That network effect is the single best reason to start here instead of a flat-fee tool.

## What Bugs Me (The Honest Cons)

- **The 10% never shrinks.** At $1,000/month paid you hand Substack $100. At $10,000/month that is $1,000 - $12,000 a year - with no volume discount and no way to negotiate it down. Flat-fee rivals (Ghost at $29/month, Beehiiv from $43/month) pass Substack on cost once you clear roughly $900/month in paid revenue.
- **Design and branding are thin.** Every Substack looks like a Substack. No drag-and-drop templates, no real theme control, limited meta-title and canonical control. If you care about a distinct brand or technical SEO, Ghost or a self-hosted setup beats it.
- **Email tooling is basic.** No drip sequences, no behavioral triggers, weak tagging, no proper A/B testing on subject lines. If you want marketing automation, this is the wrong tool - Kit or Beehiiv do that job.
- **Analytics are shallow.** You get open rates, subscriber counts, and basic revenue numbers. No cohort analysis, no click-maps, no revenue attribution by source. Fine for a writer, frustrating for a media operator.
- **The app sits between you and readers.** Substack keeps pushing its app and feed. App-only readers and Notes followers do not fully move with you if you leave. You can export your email list anytime (you own that), but the network does not follow.

## Substack vs the Alternatives

| Platform | Fee model | Best at | Weak at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Substack** | 10% of paid + Stripe | Zero-cost start, built-in reader network | Margin at scale, branding, automation |
| **Gumroad** | 10% + $0.50 + Stripe | One-off digital sales (files, prompts) | No recurring membership |
| **Patreon** | 10% + Stripe | Community memberships fans know | Discovery, email tools |
| **Whop** | 3% direct / 30% Discover | Gated communities and courses | 30% bite if Discover drives sales |
| **Beehiiv** | Flat $43/mo, 0% rev | Growth tools, analytics | No free built-in audience |
| **Ghost** | Flat $29/mo, 0% rev | Full control, SEO, branding | You build the audience yourself |

For a writer starting paid newsletters, Substack wins on cost and discovery. Once revenue is real, the math flips toward Ghost or Beehiiv.

## Getting Started (What I'd Do)

1. **Start free, publish weekly.** Pick one narrow topic and ship a useful post every week for two months. Build the list before you charge.
2. **Turn on recommendations early.** Recommend 5-10 publications in your niche and accept reciprocals. This is free growth - do not skip it.
3. **Add one paid tier at $7-10/month** once you have a few hundred engaged free readers. Keep most content free; paywall the deep or timely stuff.
4. **Push annual and founding tiers** for your superfans to lift retention and fee economics.
5. **Re-evaluate at ~$900/month paid.** If Substack's 10% now costs more than Ghost or Beehiiv's flat fee, move the hosting but keep the writing habit.

## Bottom Line

Substack is the lowest-risk way to turn writing into recurring income. You pay nothing until readers pay you, and its recommendation network does discovery that no other newsletter tool gives away free. The trade is permanent: 10% of paid revenue forever, plus thin branding and weak automation. For a writer who wants to write and get paid, that is a fair deal. For a media business optimizing margin, move on once the numbers grow.

content:
## What Ko-fi Actually Is (From Someone Who's Run a Tip Page for Years)

I've used Ko-fi since before it added memberships and a shop - back when it was just a "buy me a coffee" button you dropped on a blog. So this is written from the creator's side, not Ko-fi's sales page. Ko-fi is a monetisation hub for creators: fans send one-off tips ("coffees"), subscribe as monthly members, buy digital or physical items from your shop, or book you for commissions - all from one free page. Money lands straight in your own PayPal or Stripe account; Ko-fi never holds it.

The hook that pulled me in, and the reason it belongs in any "make money" toolkit, is the 0% tip fee. On the free plan you keep 100% of every one-off tip - Ko-fi takes nothing, you only lose the standard Stripe or PayPal processing of about 2.9% plus $0.30. A $5 coffee leaves you about $4.55. That is a lower cut than anywhere else I've tried for pure tipping.

One honest catch: new accounts now start in "Contributor" mode, which adds a 5% fee even to tips. You have to go into Payment Settings and toggle Contributor off to get the true 0% on tips. It is one click, but plenty of creators never notice and lose 5% they did not need to. I'll say it plainly so you don't.

## How People Actually Make Money On It

Ko-fi is a low-friction money funnel, not a discovery engine. The income comes from the audience you already have - readers, viewers, listeners - and the small, repeated asks you make of them:

1. **Tip jar on your existing channels.** Drop the Ko-fi button or link on your blog, YouTube description, podcast show notes, Twitch overlay, or Linktree. Fans who got value send a $3-5 coffee. Because the fee is 0%, this is the cheapest "thank you" money you can collect. A creator with 20k followers and a 0.5% tip rate pulls $300-1,000 a month from coffee buttons alone.
2. **Monthly memberships.** Set tiers at $3-10/month and reward members with Discord roles, exclusive posts, or early access. Free plan takes 5% on memberships; Ko-fi Gold ($6/month) drops that to 0%. Gold breaks even around $120/month in membership income - above that it is cheaper than the 5% cut. This is the recurring-income play that sits beside Patreon, but without Patreon's 8-12% bite.
3. **Digital shop for files you already make.** Sell prompts, templates, ebooks, Lightroom presets, notion packs, art prints - anything you can attach as a file. On the free plan shop sales take 5%; on Gold they take 0%. This is the one-off-product play that overlaps Gumroad, but Ko-fi wins if your volume is small and you already have a tipping audience.
4. **Commissions with managed slots.** If you do custom work - art, editing, consult calls - list a menu with prices and available slots. Clients pay up front, you deliver, money is already in your account. No invoicing back-and-forth.
5. **Crowdfunding goals.** Set a target (new gear, a project) and let tips fill the bar. Good for one-off community pushes.

The real strength is the funnel: a reader who tips you $5 once, with zero friction, is far easier to upsell to a $5/month membership later than someone who has never paid you at all. Ko-fi gets people into the habit of paying you directly before you ever ask for a subscription.

## Where It Falls Short (Read Before You Commit)

Ko-fi's weak spots are scale and support. Discovery is thin - its Explore page sends far less traffic than Patreon's recommendation network, so you bring your own crowd. There is no email tool, no newsletter, no drip sequences; if you want to run a mailing list you pair it with Substack or your own ESP. The shop is deliberately light: fine for a few downloads or prints, useless for dozens of SKUs or real shipping logic. And support is email-only and slow when something breaks - automated moderation has frozen accounts with little warning, which matters if your rent depends on that button.

## How Ko-fi Stacks Up Against the Rest

| Platform | Fee on tips | Fee on memberships / shop | Best at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ko-fi** | 0% (toggle off Contributor) | 5% free / 0% Gold ($6/mo) | Tipping + all-in-one for small volume |
| **Patreon** | n/a | 8-12% + Stripe | Large memberships, discovery network |
| **Gumroad** | n/a | 10% + $0.50 + Stripe | One-off digital file sales at scale |
| **Substack** | n/a | 10% + Stripe | Paid newsletters |
| **Whop** | n/a | 3% direct / 30% Discover | Gated communities and courses |
| **Buy Me a Coffee** | 0% | 5% flat (no waiver) | Simple tipping, first $100/mo free |

For pure tipping and a small shop, Ko-fi is the cheapest entry point going. Once memberships pass ~$120/month or you need serious email tools and discovery, Patreon's percentage starts to buy more.

## Getting Started (What I'd Do)

1. **Create the page, turn Contributor OFF.** Settings > Payment. This restores the 0% tip fee most people think they already have.
2. **Add the button everywhere you already have an audience.** Blog, social bios, video descriptions, email signature. Tip income comes from places you already own.
3. **Open one low-priced membership tier** at $3-5/month once a few people have tipped. Reward with a Discord role or a monthly post.
4. **List 1-2 digital products** you already have (a template, a prompt pack). Keep it light - Ko-fi's shop is not a warehouse.
5. **Re-evaluate at ~$120/month in fees.** If the 5% on memberships or shop now costs more than $6, switch on Ko-fi Gold and zero out the cut.

## Bottom Line

Ko-fi is the lowest-friction way to start collecting money from an audience you already have. The 0% tip fee is real (once you toggle off Contributor), payouts hit your own PayPal or Stripe the same day, and the free plan covers tips, a light shop, and commissions with no monthly cost. The trade is scale: discovery is weak next to Patreon, there is no email tool, and the 5% on memberships and shop only makes sense below about $120/month. For a creator who wants to turn readers and viewers into a few hundred dollars a month without building a store, Ko-fi is the first button I'd add.

content:
# MAGI-2 Review: The First Hundred-Billion-Parameter Open-Source Video Model With Built-In Sound

MAGI-2 is Sand.ai's open-source video generation model, released on August 5, 2026. It takes a text prompt — or a text prompt plus a starting image — and produces a 10-second 1080p video with audio that is synchronized to the action. With 114 billion total parameters in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture that activates only about 6 billion per token, it is the first video model at the hundred-billion scale to publish both its weights and its inference code under the Apache 2.0 license. If you want video-with-sound generation that you can run, fine-tune, and ship inside your own stack without per-clip API billing, this is the release to watch.

## What Makes MAGI-2 Different

Most open video models generate silent clips. You run the video model, then pipe the result into a separate audio model, then align the two in post. MAGI-2 removes that pipeline. Text, video, and audio tokens are concatenated into a single sequence and processed by one Transformer backbone, so speech, lip movement, body motion, ambient sound, and camera rhythm exchange information throughout the model rather than only at a narrow cross-attention step. The model renders the visuals and the soundtrack in a single pass, then muxes the audio into the output MP4.

The practical payoff is coherence: a character who starts speaking has mouth movement that matches the generated voice, and environmental sound (footsteps, water, wind) tracks the on-screen motion instead of being bolted on afterward.

## Architecture: 114B Capacity, 6B Active

MAGI-2 uses a fine-grained MoE design. Each token's representation is split into 12 latent heads of 256 dimensions; each head runs its own router and selects its top-6 experts from a pool of 256 narrow experts. That yields 3,072 head-local expert units per sparse layer, of which only 72 activate per token. The result is a model with the capacity of 114B parameters but the per-token compute of roughly 6B — which is why its reported inference cost at scale is around ¥0.5 (about $0.07) per 10-second clip, roughly a tenth of comparable proprietary APIs.

Generation is two-stage: a preview stage renders at 512×896, then a refiner stage upscales to 1088×1920 (approximately 1080p). The only supported duration in this preview release is 10 seconds.

## How to Run MAGI-2

MAGI-2 is self-hosted. There is no hosted API yet (one is expected), so you run it yourself:

1. **Hardware**: 8× NVIDIA Hopper GPUs (H100 or equivalent). This is a hard requirement for the full model; quantized or distilled variants for smaller rigs are not available in the preview.
2. **Get the code**: clone `github.com/SandAI-org/MAGI-2-preview`.
3. **Download weights**: `hf download sand-ai/MAGI-2-preview --local-dir ckpt` (about 307 GB: 228 GB preview transformer, 14 GB refiner, 56 GB Qwen3.5-27B text encoder, plus video/audio VAEs and a distilled turbo VAE decoder). A Docker image is provided.
4. **Run inference**: `bash scripts/run_demo.sh` launches the pipeline under `torchrun` across all visible GPUs, generating at 1080p from a samples JSON file. Output lands as `sample_000.mp4`, `sample_001.mp4`, and so on.
5. **Prompt enhancement (optional)**: MAGI-2 was trained on long, structured captions. A short prompt underuses it. The repo ships a prompt-enhancement (PE) step that calls an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint to expand your prompt into a structured JSON caption; leave the API key empty to skip PE and use your raw prompt.

There are no ComfyUI custom nodes for MAGI-2 at the time of writing, so expect a command-line workflow rather than a node graph.

## MAGI-2 vs Other AI Video Tools

| Dimension | MAGI-2 | Kling AI | Runway | Sora | MiniMax H3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source weights | ✅ (Apache 2.0) | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Built-in audio | ✅ (single-stream) | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Max clip | 10s | 10s | 10s | 20s | longer |
| 1080p | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Runs on 8×H100 | required | API/cloud | API/cloud | API/cloud | API/cloud |
| Cost model | self-host GPU | subscription | subscription | subscription | subscription |

The honest takeaway: [Kling AI](/kling-ai/) and [Runway](/runway/) win on accessibility and turnaround today, and [Sora](/sora/) leads on maximum clip length. MAGI-2 wins on two things that matter for builders — it is fully open (you own the stack) and it generates synchronized audio natively. On the Artificial Analysis video leaderboard it sits around 6th, competitive with far larger proprietary systems.

## Who Should Use MAGI-2

- **Studios and agencies** that already run GPU clusters and want to stop paying per-clip API fees for ad, short-drama, or animation production.
- **Researchers** who need a transparent, modifiable video foundation model to study scaling, audio-visual alignment, or fine-tuning.
- **Product teams** building proprietary video features who cannot send source footage to a third-party API.

If you just want to make a quick social clip, [Pika](/pika/), [PixVerse](/pixverse/), [Seedance](/seedance/), or [Vidu AI](/vidu-ai/) are faster to start. MAGI-2 is a build-it-yourself foundation, not a SaaS.

## Limitations

- **Hardware barrier**: 8× Hopper GPUs and ~307 GB of weights make it inaccessible without serious infrastructure.
- **Preview maturity**: this is a preview release; the full distilled version (far fewer denoising steps) is "coming soon."
- **10-second ceiling**: longer narratives require stitching multiple clips.
- **No hosted API yet**: you must operate the inference pipeline yourself.

## FAQ

### Is MAGI-2 free?

Yes. The weights and code are released under Apache 2.0, so you can use, modify, and commercialize output without per-clip licensing fees. The cost is your own GPU compute.

### Who made MAGI-2?

MAGI-2 was developed by Sand.ai, following MAGI-1, its autoregressive video model from April 2025. The preview release validates that its architecture and training system scale together at the 100B level.

### How much does it cost to run?

There is no API bill. Reported inference cost at scale is about ¥0.5 (≈$0.07) per 10-second clip on owned hardware, roughly a tenth of comparable proprietary APIs — but you must supply the GPUs.

### Can MAGI-2 generate audio?

Yes. Audio is generated natively in the same pass as the video, with lip movement and ambient sound synchronized to the visuals.

### Where do I get MAGI-2?

Weights: `huggingface.co/sand-ai/MAGI-2-preview`. Code: `github.com/SandAI-org/MAGI-2-preview`. Announcement: `sand.ai/blog/magi-2-preview`.

## Final Assessment

MAGI-2 is the most important open video release of 2026 for one reason: it is the first hundred-billion-parameter video model you can actually own. The hardware requirement is steep, and the hosted API is not here yet, but for teams with GPUs it collapses "generate video" and "generate sound" into a single open pipeline. Watch the distilled release — that is when MAGI-2 becomes practical for most builders.

content:
## What Skool Actually Is (From Someone Running a Paid Group)

I've run a paid Skool community for two years, and before that I burnt months on a Facebook Group, a Discord, and a Patreon that never quite clicked. So this is written from the owner's chair, not Skool's brochure. Skool crams three things into one app: a community feed, a course area they call the Classroom, and a calendar. Members pay you a recurring or one-time fee to get in, and Skool handles the billing through Stripe. The part that hooked me was the points system - members level up by posting and reacting, and a leaderboard sits at the top of the group. It sounds like a sticker chart for adults, but it works: my quiet members started posting because they wanted the next level.

## How People Make Money on It

Skool is not a traffic source. It's the place you send people who already trust you. The four ways I've seen creators turn it into income:

1. **Coaching and masterminds.** Charge $99-497/month for a group where you run weekly calls and answer questions. This is the most common Skool business and the one with the best margins, because the $99 platform fee stays flat no matter how many join.
2. **Course plus community.** Sell a course, but host it inside Skool and wrap a paid group around it. Completion rates beat a lonely Teachable course because the feed pulls people back.
3. **Free group as a funnel.** Run one free community (you still pay $99/month to host it) as a lead magnet, then pitch a paid group inside it. Most big Skool operators run exactly this two-layer setup.
4. **Affiliate income.** Skool pays a 40% recurring commission if you refer other creators. It's one of the better affiliate deals around, and it pairs naturally with a 'how I built my community' content trail.

## The Fee Math, Spelled Out

On the Pro plan Skool charges a flat $99/month and takes **0%** of what your members pay. Stripe takes its normal ~2.9% + $0.30 per transaction. That's the whole cut. Compare that to Patreon (8-12% plus processing), Whop (up to 30% on its marketplace), or Substack (10% plus Stripe). On a $5,000/month community, Skool saves you roughly $400-600 a month versus Patreon and thousands versus Whop.

Break-even is easy to picture:

- $10/month price -> about 11 members to cover the fee
- $35/month -> about 3 members
- $99/month -> about 1 member
- $500/month mastermind -> one member pays for the whole platform with room to spare

One caveat on price: a few 2026 reviews mention a cheaper 'Hobby' tier around $9/month that adds a 10% transaction fee. Skool changes plans by region, so check skool.com for what's live where you are before you commit. The 14-day trial needs no credit card to build, which is the rare honest trial in this space. Payouts run through Stripe Connect on a rolling schedule, and your first payout can take up to two weeks to clear.

## Where It Falls Short

I'll be straight about the annoyances, because they bit me:

- **No built-in email or automation.** Want a welcome DM, a churn alert when someone cancels, or a tagged segment? None of it exists natively. Past ~80 paying members I was doing manual ops until I wired Zapier and ConvertKit on top - more subscriptions, more bills.
- **The course tools are bare.** No quizzes, no certificates, no drip scheduling, no completion tracking. If you teach accredited or structured material, Skool will feel thin and you'll want Teachable or Kajabi beside it.
- **One price per community.** You can't run Basic/Premium/VIP inside a single group. Three tiers means three $99/month communities. The cost stacks fast if you like to segment.
- **Stripe only, skool.com branding.** No PayPal, no ACH. Your group lives on a skool.com address with Skool's logo always showing - you can't white-label it as your own product.
- **$99 hits even when you're not earning.** A tiny or free community still pays the full fee. If you're pre-audience, that $99 stings before any member joins.

## Skool vs the Other Platforms I've Used

| If you want to... | Pick | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run a paid community + course with 0% cut | **Skool** | Flat $99, gamification keeps it alive, native apps |
| Simple fan club with some discovery | Patreon | Easier tiers, brings a little reach |
| Sell one-off files, prompts, templates | Gumroad | Cheapest checkout, no monthly fee |
| Paid newsletter from your writing | Substack | Built for newsletters, recommendation network |
| Sell products on a storefront | Whop | Product focus, but up to 30% marketplace fee |
| Free tips while you grow | Ko-fi | 0% on tips, free to start |

None of these replace the others. I run Skool for the community and keep Gumroad for one-off downloads - the two do different jobs.

## How I'd Start If I Were You

1. Take the 14-day trial seriously - build the group skeleton, post three lessons, invite three friends to test.
2. Pick one offer and one price. $29-49/month is the sweet spot for a first paid group; don't launch five tiers.
3. Move your most engaged people in first. A live group beats an empty one, so seed it with real members before you open the door.
4. Set up one automated bridge (Zapier -> your email tool) so new members land on your list. Do this on day one, not after you're drowning in DMs.
5. Show up weekly. Skool's whole bet is that a steady host keeps a group active - if you go quiet, the leaderboard goes quiet too.

Skool won't make you money by itself. It just stops the platform from taking a cut while you build the thing that does.

If you already have even a few thousand warm followers, that is the cheapest way to start selling your own digital products without building a website.
pros: Zero platform cut - you keep 100% of every sale after Stripe. On a $97 template sold 20 times a month you clear about $1,882; Gumroad's free plan would take roughly $194 of that. The flat fee pays for itself once you pass about $300 a month in sales.
Fast to launch - I had a live, purchase-ready page in under 30 minutes: upload a file, connect Stripe, set a price, share the link. No separate course host, no Calendly, no open Gumroad tab.

The bio-link format converts social traffic - when your whole audience lives in Stories and Reels, a single page with visible product tiles beats sending them to a multi-page site. The embedded one-tap checkout is built for the phone-in-hand buyer.

Course hosting and bookings included even on the $29 plan - you can host a video mini-course and take coaching calls on the same page, so a solo creator avoids paying for Teachable plus a scheduling tool.
Instagram AutoDMs pull the buyer into your world - set a keyword and Stan DMs the purchaser or lead-magnet downloader, which is a clean way to keep the relationship going off the platform.
cons: No free plan - you pay $29 a month before your first sale. For a total beginner with no audience yet, that is a real monthly bill with no guaranteed return, and Stan sends you no traffic.

The math that works: a fitness coach selling a $37 PDF workout plan to 2,000 engaged followers at a 2% conversion is 40 sales a month, about $1,450 gross, nearly all of it yours after Stripe. Most creators I know use Stan for the social storefront and link out to the others for specific jobs.

content:
## What Stan Store Actually Is (From Someone Who Sells From a Bio Link)

I have sold digital products from a Stan Store for over a year, before that from a Gumroad tab and a Linktree that sent people everywhere but the checkout. So this is written from the seller's chair, not Stan's marketing page. Stan does one job: it takes the single link you get in your Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube bio and turns it into a real store. Visitors see product tiles, tap one, and pay right there on their phone. No website, no separate course platform, no scheduling tool to wire up.

The reason it caught on with creators is the fee model. Most link-in-bio tools are free or cheap but then take a cut of sales, or they don't sell at all. Stan flips it: you pay a flat monthly fee and it takes nothing from your sales. For someone already posting to a warm audience every day, that is the cheapest on-ramp to selling your own stuff.

## How People Make Money on It

Stan is not a traffic source. It is the page you send people who already trust you. The four ways I have seen creators turn it into income:

1. **Digital downloads for a social-native audience.** PDF guides, Lightroom presets, Canva templates, prompt packs, Notion dashboards. Upload once, set a price, and delivery is automatic. A TikTok creator with 50k followers selling a $17 preset pack at 100 sales a month clears about $1,650 with almost no work after the first upload.

2. **Coaching and consultation bookings.** The built-in calendar takes payment at booking, so you stop paying for Calendly. A fitness or business coach bundles a $37 PDF with a $200 one-on-one call and fills the week from Reels alone.

3. **Mini-courses hosted on the page.** Even the $29 plan hosts video modules. A $197 course promoted through Instagram Reels at a 2% conversion on 10k followers is 200 sales a month - roughly $39k gross, and Stan takes none of it beyond Stripe.

4. **Memberships and recurring packs on Pro.** The $99 plan adds subscriptions, so you can drop a fresh pack of prompts or templates each month at near-zero marginal cost. This is the same play Patreon users run, but the checkout lives in your bio instead of a separate site.

## What I Like and What I Don't

The good: setup is genuinely fast. I went from sign-up to a live, purchase-ready store in under half an hour. The one-tap mobile checkout converts better than a multi-page site because the buyer never leaves the app. And the 0% cut is real - on a $97 product sold 20 times a month I keep about $1,882; Gumroad's free plan would skim roughly $194 of that.

The rough edges are just as real. There is no free plan, so you pay $29 before your first sale - fine if you already earn, rough if you are starting cold. Email automation (sequences, tagging, behavioral flows) is locked behind the $99 Pro tier, so the $29 plan is really a capture-and-broadcast tool; if you want funnels you pay double or add Kit and pay for that too. Every store looks near-identical - limited templates, no custom domain on any plan, so there is no SEO and no brand control over the URL. And Stan gives you no discovery; all traffic is on you. The people who quit and call it a scam usually never had an audience to send in the first place.

## Stan Store vs the Other Tools Covered Here

This site already covers the rest of the creator-income stack, and they are not competitors so much as different jobs:

- **Gumroad** - cheapest for one-off file sales (free to start, 10% on the free plan) but sends buyers to a separate checkout site.
- **Patreon** - best for a simple fan club with some discovery; takes a flat ~10% plus processing.
- **Substack** - the paid-newsletter path; 10% of paid plus Stripe.
- **Whop** - product storefront, up to 30% on its marketplace.
- **Ko-fi** - free tipping hub, 0% on tips.
- **Skool** - paid community plus course, 0% on Pro at a flat $99.

Stan's lane is the social storefront: when your buyers live in Stories and Reels, it is the fastest way from follower to customer. Use Gumroad for file delivery off-platform, Patreon for the fan club, Skool for the community, and Stan for the bio-link sale.

## How to Start (If You Already Have an Audience)

1. Sign up at stan.store and start the 14-day trial - no card needed to build.
2. Connect Stripe (or PayPal) so you can take payments; this is the only per-sale cost, about 2.9% plus $0.30.
3. Upload one paid product you can deliver automatically - a PDF, a preset pack, or a short video course.
4. Turn on Instagram AutoDMs with a keyword so buyers and lead-magnet grabbers get pulled into a DM.
5. Put the Stan link in your bio and mention it in every post for a week; watch which product tiles get taps and double down on that one.

If you have under ~2,000 engaged followers, hold off - pay for the audience first, then the store. If you already post to a warm crowd daily, Stan is the quickest $29 you will spend to start keeping 100% of your sales.

content:
## What Hedra actually does

Hedra turns a single portrait or character image plus an audio clip into a talking video. You upload a face, drop in a voice file (or type a script and let its text-to-speech read it), and the Character-1 model animates the mouth, eyes, and head movement to match the audio. I have used it for client explainer videos and for building a faceless YouTube channel, and the lip sync is noticeably better than what I got out of D-ID a year ago.

The honest part: it is not a full video editor. It makes talking-head clips. If you want B-roll, transitions, and a finished timeline, you still need CapCut or DaVinci. Hedra handles the talking character; the rest is on you.

## How people make money with Hedra

This is the part most reviews skip. A talking avatar is only worth something if it saves you paid work or opens a revenue stream. A few that actually pay:

- **Faceless channels.** YouTube and TikTok pay through ads and brand deals once you hold an audience. A consistent avatar lets you post daily without a camera, a studio, or showing your face. The risk is real: shorts saturation is high, and watch time still decides revenue.
- **UGC ad creatives.** Small brands burn through ad variants. You can sell 10 to 20 talking-avatar ad scripts a week at $50 to $200 each, using the client own spokesperson image with their voice clone. Margin is high because generation is cheap.
- **Agency video work.** Local gyms, dentists, and coaches need simple spokes-character videos. Hedra plus ElevenLabs [voice cloning](/tools/elevenlabs/) gets you there without hiring a videographer.
- **Course and product demos.** If you sell an info product, a reusable character that narrates updates saves you re-recording screen captures every time pricing changes.

None of these are passive. The tool removes production cost; it does not bring customers.

## Where it falls short

- **Length caps.** Each clip is short (under a minute on lower tiers). Long videos mean stitching multiple generations, and the face can drift between clips.
- **One character per render.** No multi-person conversation in a single take. You generate separately and edit together.
- **Free tier is thin.** You get limited monthly generations with a watermark. Commercial work needs a paid plan.
- **Expressiveness varies by input.** A clean, front-facing photo gives the best result. A low-res or heavily filtered image looks rough.

## Pricing

Freemium. A free plan exists with limited generations and a watermark. Paid plans start around $15/month and open up commercial rights, higher resolution, and more generations. Treat the free tier as a test drive, not a production tool.

## How it compares

For realistic human spokespeople at business scale, [HeyGen](/tools/heygen/) is the safer pick. For enterprise training video, [Synthesia](/tools/synthesia/) leads. Hedra wins on character expressiveness and on illustrated or stylized avatars that other tools mangle. If your work is character-driven rather than corporate, it is the stronger choice.

## FAQ

**Can I use my own voice in Hedra?**
Yes. Upload a recorded audio file or clone a voice on paid plans. You are not locked to its built-in text-to-speech.

**Is the free plan usable for commercial projects?**
No. The free tier adds a watermark and caps generations. Paid plans from about $15/month include commercial rights.

**Does Hedra work with illustrated or cartoon characters?**
Better than most. It generalizes to stylized art, mascots, and AI-generated portraits, which makes it useful for animated brand spokes-characters.

**What file do I get out?**
Usually 1080p MP4. Background can be transparent, blurred, or AI-filled, which helps when you drop the character into another edit.

## Bottom line

Hedra is a focused tool that does one job well: making a still image talk convincingly. It will not replace your editor, and the free tier will not run a business. But if you need talking-avatar video at volume for ads, faceless content, or client work, it is one of the cheapest ways to produce it. Start on the free plan, confirm the face quality on your own images, then upgrade only when a paying job justifies it.

content:
## What Kajabi Is (From Someone Who's Paid The Bill)

I've run a paid course and a small membership on Kajabi, so this is field notes, not a brochure. Kajabi is the all-in-one box for selling knowledge: it hosts your course, sends your email, builds your funnel, serves your site, and runs your community, all from one login. The pitch is simple — stop paying for five tools and write one bill instead.

Where it clicked for me: I was paying for a course host, an email app, and a landing-page builder, and they never talked to each other. A sale in one didn't tag the contact in the other. On Kajabi, the sale, the email, and the funnel are the same record. That alone saved me a weekly 'why didn't this automation fire' session.

## How People Actually Make Money On Kajabi

The platform is neutral. The income comes from what you sell. What works:

### 1. Paid Courses (The Core)
Package a skill into video modules with quizzes and a completion certificate. Price it $99–$499 one-time or $20–$80/mo. A 200-student course at $199 is ~$40k, and you deliver it once. The margin beats trading hours for dollars.

### 2. Memberships and Communities
Recurring access to a group, a library, or coaching calls. Set a monthly price, Kajabi gates the community, and cancels cut access automatically. A 100-member group at $29/mo is $2,900 in steady revenue — if you keep showing up.

### 3. Coaching and Hybrid Offers
Sell one-on-one or group calls through Kajabi's scheduling, bundled with a course. Good for high-ticket: a $1,500 coaching package with a $200 course attached feels like a deal and lifts your take.

### 4. Funnels and Order Bumps
Build a free quiz or lead magnet, then a sales page with an order bump and an upsell. Kajabi's pipelines do this without a separate funnel tool. The bump alone often covers the monthly fee.

### 5. Affiliates
Turn buyers into referrers on Growth and up. They get a link, you set the cut, Kajabi tracks and pays. Cheap word-of-mouth at scale.

## The Features That Earn Their Keep

- **Course player with certificates.** Video, quizzes, progress tracking, and a completion cert — enough for most paid academies.
- **Email under the same roof.** Broadcasts and sequences tied to purchases. No Zapier bridge to a separate app.
- **Pipelines.** Prebuilt funnel templates with upsells and one-click checkout. Launch in an afternoon.
- **Site and blog builder.** A real homepage and blog, so you don't also need WordPress.
- **Branded app + no Kajabi logo** on Growth and up. Your business looks like yours.

## The Honest Downsides

I won't soften these, because they cost real money:

1. **No free tier, and the real plan starts near $179/mo.** If you're pre-revenue, that's rent on an empty shop. Kajabi only makes sense once sales cover the bill.
2. **The '0% fee' has an asterisk.** Zero platform fee only on Kajabi Payments. Wire your own Stripe and a 2% surcharge stacks on top of card processing (~2.9% + $0.30), so a Basic-plan sale runs about 4.9% + $0.30. Use Kajabi Payments, or price the surcharge in.
3. **Caps push you up tiers.** Basic allows 5 products and 2,500 contacts. A modest email list and a few offers, and you're shopping for Growth at $249/mo.
4. **You pay for the whole bundle even if you use half.** Solo sellers who only need a course host often overpay versus Teachable or Podia.
5. **You live in their walls.** Leave Kajabi and you rebuild funnels, email, and member data elsewhere. Keep a list export on hand.
6. **Prices moved in 2026.** Kajabi raised several tiers and added metered AI credit add-ons. The number you see today may not be the number next quarter — verify before you commit.

## Kajabi vs the Others

| Tool | Best for | Weak spot | Cost |
|------|----------|-----------|------|
| Kajabi | Full course + email + funnel stack | Pricey, no free tier | From ~$179/mo |
| Teachable | Course hosting, cheaper entry | Thin email/funnel tools | From ~$39/mo |
| Podia | Simple courses + downloads | Lighter automation | From ~$39/mo |
| [Whop](/tools/whop/) | Gated communities, free start | Thin courses, 30% marketplace fee | 3% direct |
| [Gumroad](/tools/gumroad/) | One-file downloads | Weak community | ~10% |

Pick Kajabi when you want one dashboard and you can cover the bill from day one. Pick Teachable or Podia when you're earlier and price matters more than the bundle.

## Starting Without Burning Cash

1. **Take the 14-day trial.** Build one course and one funnel. Don't migrate everything yet.
2. **Price to clear the fee.** At $179/mo you need ~$200+ in course revenue before you break even. Charge enough.
3. **Use Kajabi Payments** to keep the 0% platform fee; avoid the Stripe surcharge unless you have a reason.
4. **Turn on the affiliate program** the day you launch. Happy buyers are your cheapest ads.
5. **Keep your list exported.** Own your audience data outside Kajabi.
6. **Start with one paid offer** you can deliver today — not a 12-module mega-course.

## The Bottom Line

Kajabi is the most complete single dashboard I've used for selling courses, memberships, and coaching. It replaces three or four subscriptions and the glue between them, and the 0% fee on its own processor is real.

The catch is the bill: no free tier, a steep entry, and tier caps that pull you upward as you grow. It pays off once you have an audience and steady sales — not before. If you're pre-revenue, start on Teachable or Podia and move up when the income justifies it. If you're already selling, Kajabi is one of the cleaner ways to run the whole machine from one place.

faq.question: Lemon Squeezy or Gumroad or Paddle?

faq.question: Can I still sign up in 2026?

content:
## What Lemon Squeezy Is (From A Maker Who's Used It)

I've shipped a small software license and a template pack through Lemon Squeezy, so this is field notes, not a sales page. Lemon Squeezy is a merchant of record: when someone buys from you, Lemon Squeezy is the legal seller on the receipt. That one detail is the whole point. Because they're the seller, they calculate, collect, and file VAT, GST, and sales tax in more than 200 jurisdictions. You price in dollars, someone in Germany buys, and you never register for a German VAT number or hire a tax service. For a solo maker selling across borders, the removal of that paperwork is worth more than the fee looks at first glance.

## How People Actually Make Money On It

The tool is just the checkout. The income is what you put behind it. What works:

### 1. Sell A Digital File, Once, Forever
An ebook, a Figma template, a Lightroom preset, a Notion dashboard, a sprite pack. Upload it, set a price of $9 to $49, and Lemon Squeezy delivers the file and handles tax on every country. A pack that sells 300 times at $19 is about $5,700, and you made it once. The 5% + 50¢ is the cost of not running a tax department.

### 2. License Keys For Software And Plugins
This is where Lemon Squeezy beats a plain processor. It generates and validates license keys out of the box, so if you sell a WordPress plugin, a desktop app, or a CLI tool, buyers get a working key at checkout and you get renewals without glue code. Subscriptions add 0.5%, but for software that is expected.

### 3. Turn Buyers Into Resellers
The built-in affiliate program is the part most people skip. Give a customer a tracked link, set a 20 to 30% commission, and they send you buyers for a cut of the sale. You pay only after money comes in. For a maker with an audience, this is cheaper customer acquisition than ads, and it runs while you sleep.

### 4. Recurring Revenue Without The Tax Headache
Subscriptions for a SaaS, a preset club, or a monthly asset drop. Lemon Squeezy bills, duns failed cards, and files the cross-border tax. The catch: the subscription surcharge plus international and PayPal fees can push a European PayPal sub to about 9%, so price for it or steer buyers to cards.

## Where It Bites

Read the fee stack before you celebrate. The base is 5% + 50¢. International cards add 1.5%. PayPal adds 1.5%. Subscriptions add 0.5%. On a $5 product the fixed 50¢ alone is 10%, and the surcharges push it to 15%. Lemon Squeezy is a poor fit for high-volume, low-ticket items. There the flat fee eats you. It is also not your business shell: no course host, no community, no funnel builder. It moves money. Pair it with a host for the rest.

And the 2026 reality check: the platform is live, but new signups have been reported as gated, and it stopped taking new mainland-China developer applications after Stripe bought it in 2024. Its tech now feeds Stripe Managed Payments, a costlier successor. If you can't open an account, the features don't matter. Have Paddle or Polar ready as a fallback.

## Who Should Reach For It

Pick Lemon Squeezy when you sell software, license keys, or digital downloads and want tax filed for you plus an affiliate engine, without a monthly bill. Skip it if you're moving thousands of $5 items, the fixed fee hurts, or if you need a full course-and-community platform. For a maker shipping a product to the world from a laptop, it removes the single most annoying part of going global: the tax.

## What Polar Is (From A Builder Who's Watched It Closely)

I haven't shipped a product on Polar yet, but I've wired up its SDK and read enough post-mortems to call it like it is. Polar is a merchant of record and billing stack for people who sell software, SaaS, and AI products. When a customer pays, Polar is the legal seller on the receipt. That one line is the whole pitch: because they're the seller, they collect and remit VAT, GST, and sales tax across 100+ markets, and the liability sits on their name, not yours.

For a solo dev or a two-person AI startup, that removes the single biggest reason most people never sell outside their home country. You price in dollars, someone in Germany buys, and you never register for a German VAT number or hire a cross-border tax service.

## How People Actually Make Money On It

Polar is the checkout and billing layer. The income is what you put behind it. What works:

### 1. Sell A Token-Metered API
This is Polar's standout use. If you wrap a model and charge per call, Polar meters tokens, API requests, and GPU seconds in real time and bills them on the next invoice. No custom usage engine, no Stripe usage records glue code. A wrapper that goes viral on a weekend bills itself correctly without you touching a calculator. The LLM ingestion strategy plugs straight into the Vercel AI SDK, so the meter fills from your existing calls.

### 2. License A CLI Tool Or Desktop App
Polar generates and validates license keys out of the box and delivers them the instant payment clears. Sell a $29 WordPress plugin, a $15 CLI, or a $49 desktop app and the buyer gets a working key at checkout. Subscriptions carry no separate surcharge on Polar's plans, so recurring revenue stays simple.

### 3. Run A SaaS With Seats And Usage
Mix fixed seats with usage caps. Polar handles trials, proration, and dunning, and its cost-insights view shows true gross margin per customer, tying your inference cost to what each one pays. That view is the part most billing tools skip: it tells you which $20 plans are quietly burning $60 of tokens.

### 4. Monetize Open Source
Set a pay-what-you-want tier or a funded tier, and Polar grants GitHub repo access or Discord roles on payment. Open-source maintainers use it to turn GitHub stars into recurring income without building a storefront.

## Where It Beats The Alternatives

The developer experience is the differentiator. Python and TypeScript SDKs, webhooks, and Next.js adapters get a basic checkout live in an afternoon, often under ten lines of code. Pricing is posted in public, no sales call, and you switch plans and the rate changes the same day.

Compared with Lemon Squeezy (5% + 50¢, close on paper) and Paddle (blended rate, no card surcharge but slower onboarding), Polar wins on usage billing and transparency for software. It's open source under Apache 2.0, with advisors from Vercel and HashiCorp, which counts when you're trusting a 2023 startup with revenue.

## The Honest Downsides

The base fee is high because merchant-of-record service is bundled in. On Starter (5% + 50¢) a $5 sale loses about 15% to fees, and the paid plans only save money past roughly $1,400 (Pro), $5,600 (Growth), or $19,000 (Scale) in monthly sales. International non-US cards add 1.5%; disputes cost $15 each; payouts carry Stripe's own pass-through fees. A European card sale can land near 6.5% + fees on Starter.

New accounts opened after May 27, 2026 start at the worse 5% + 50¢ rate; the cheaper 4% + 40¢ legacy tier is gone for fresh signups. And the ecosystem is young, fewer integrations and a smaller community than Paddle or Stripe, with some marketing and analytics tooling still missing. It also handles software and digital goods only, no physical products.

## Who Should Use It

If you sell a token API, a SaaS, or a license key, Polar is the most developer-friendly checkout you can stand up in a day. If you're early and selling cheap items, Starter's fee will pinch, and a raw Stripe setup might be cheaper until volume climbs. Treat it as your billing layer, not your bank: withdraw on schedule, and keep Paddle or Stripe as a fallback so one platform's policy change can't freeze your income.

name: Fourthwall
description: Fourthwall is an all-in-one storefront for creators who already have an audience on YouTube, Twitch, or TikTok and want to turn that reach into recurring income. It runs print-on-demand merch, paid memberships, digital downloads, and tips from one branded site you own, with no monthly fee until you sell. For a streamer or video creator it replaces Patreon plus a merch vendor plus a tip jar with a single checkout that carries your name, not a marketplace's.
price: Free $0/mo (5% memberships, 0% self-shipped merch) / Pro $19 per month
pros: No monthly fee to start, and the storefront is yours. The Free plan costs $0/mo; you pay 5% on memberships and digital products, 0% on self-shipped and catalog merch (you keep the markup above base cost). Against Patreon's 10% standard tier, a $5,000 membership month loses about $250 to Fourthwall versus $500 to Patreon. The site runs on your domain with your design, so the brand stays with you instead of a platform that inserts its own logo.

Merch without inventory or upfront cost. The catalog has 200+ print-on-demand products (apparel, drinkware, home decor) with fulfillment and customer support handled for you. You set the price, keep the spread above the listed base cost, and never buy stock. A $10-cost tee sold at $25 nets you $15 minus processing. Good for testing drops without risking cash on a pre-order.

Memberships beat Patreon on the fee and the feature set. Tiers include members-only video, audio, image posts, polls, and Discord roles, plus a member app. The 5% cut undercuts Patreon's 8-12% and matches Ko-fi's 5%, but adds a real storefront layer Ko-fi lacks. For creators who want community plus a shop in one place, it closes the gap those tools leave open.

Deep native integrations with where your audience already is. YouTube Merch Shelf, TikTok Shop, Twitch Gifting, and Discord connect directly, so fans buy without leaving the platform they follow you on. Email and SMS marketing, Zapier, and Kit/Klaviyo/Mailchimp/beehiiv round out the funnel, and you own the customer data rather than renting it.

Backed and proven at scale. Founded 2019, $17M raised (Lightspeed, Initialized, Seven Seven Six), with YouTuber Phil DeFranco as Chief Creative Officer. DeFranco said his merch revenue grew tenfold after moving over, and 500,000+ creators use it (MKBHD among them). Trustpilot sits at 4.4/5 across 347 reviews as of August 2026.
cons: The 'branded mobile app' is a web app, not a real App Store listing. Fourthwall's own help center confirms the member app is a mobile web app you install from a browser with push notifications, not a native iOS/Android app on the stores. If you wanted an owned distribution channel in the App Store, you don't get one here.

Merch quality is inconsistent across reviews. Trustpilot and several review sites flag wrong colors, print defects, and long production times on some orders. Because Fourthwall uses outside manufacturing partners, print quality varies by item and region, and you wear the brand damage when a fan receives a bad shirt.

The 5% membership fee does not go away on Pro. Pro ($19/mo) drops digital products to 0% but memberships still pay 5%, plus 2.9% + $0.30 card processing on every US transaction. On 1,000 members at $5, card fees alone take about $445/mo, so all-in cost lands near 14% - fair, but not free, and Pro does not fix the membership cut.

No built-in discovery or marketplace traffic. Fourthwall is a storefront, not a community like Etsy or a feed like TikTok. You bring the audience; if you start cold, the platform sends zero buyers. Creators who expect organic reach will stall until they drive traffic themselves.

Support runs thin at times. Multiple reviews mention slow replies or no reply on order issues, and the Free plan has no priority support. When a shipment goes missing during a launch, you may wait while customers complain to you, not to Fourthwall.

faq.question: How do I actually make money with Fourthwall?
faq.answer: You connect it to an audience you already reach, then pick one or more revenue streams on a single branded site. The clearest plays: sell print-on-demand merch and keep the markup above each item's listed base cost (a $10-cost tee at $25 nets you $15 before card fees); run paid memberships at 5% for member-only video, audio, and Discord roles; sell digital products like presets or ebooks (5% on Free, 0% on Pro); and take tips at 0%. Wire it to YouTube Merch Shelf, TikTok Shop, or Twitch Gifting so fans buy without leaving the platform. The money compounds when the same follower buys a shirt, joins a tier, and grabs a template - one audience, three checkout paths, no extra tools.

faq.question: What does Fourthwall cost, really?
faq.answer: Free plan is $0/mo. You pay 5% on memberships and digital products, 0% on self-shipped and catalog merch (you keep the price-over-base-cost spread), and 2.9% + $0.30 per US card transaction. Pro is $19/mo (or $180/yr) and drops digital products to 0% but memberships still cost 5%. Run the math on a $5,000 membership month: Fourthwall takes $250 plus about $445 in card fees, you keep ~$4,305 (all-in near 14%). Patreon's 10% standard tier would take $500 plus the same processing. On low volume the Free plan is cheaper than a raw Shopify sub plus apps, but the 5% membership cut never disappears.

faq.question: Fourthwall, Patreon, or Ko-fi for memberships?
faq.answer: All three take about 5% on memberships, but the package differs. Patreon's standard new-creator tier is 10%, so Fourthwall undercuts it on fee, yet Patreon has the larger built-in audience and simpler onboarding. Ko-fi matches the 5% but stays a tip-and-membership tool with no real storefront. Fourthwall's edge is the storefront plus POD merch plus digital products in one owned domain - if you want community AND a shop under your brand, it wins; if you only need a donation page, Ko-fi is lighter; if you want maximum discovery, Patreon still has the bigger built-in crowd.

faq.question: Is the Fourthwall mobile app on the App Store?
faq.answer: No. The member 'app' Fourthwall promotes is a mobile web app (PWA) your subscribers install from a browser with push notifications - it is not a native app listed on the iOS App Store or Google Play. Fourthwall's help center states this directly. It works for member feeds and alerts, but it is not an owned distribution asset in the stores, and Apple or Google can't reject or remove it because it was never submitted. If a true native app matters to your strategy, budget for a separate build.

## What Fourthwall Is (From A Creator Who's Watched It Closely)

I've built stores on a couple of these platforms and tracked Fourthwall since Phil DeFranco went public with it. Fourthwall is an all-in-one commerce layer for creators who already have an audience and want to monetize it without stitching together five tools. When a fan buys, the transaction runs through a branded checkout on your domain, and Fourthwall handles production, shipping, and order support for physical merch behind the scenes.

The pitch is ownership of the storefront. Your design, your domain, your customer data, no marketplace logo sitting between you and the buyer. For a YouTuber, streamer, or musician who has spent years earning trust, that layer matters more than another 2% in fees.

## How People Actually Make Money On It

Fourthwall is the storefront and fulfillment; the income is what you point at it. What works:

### 1. Sell Print-On-Demand Merch And Keep The Markup
This is the default play. The catalog spans 200+ products (tees, hoodies, hats, mugs, posters, decor) with fulfillment and support handled for you. Each item has a listed base cost; you set the retail price and keep the spread. A $10-cost tee sold at $25 nets you $15 before card fees, with zero inventory risk. Good for testing a drop on a whim - if it flops, you lost nothing but the design time.

### 2. Run Paid Memberships
Tiers open member-only video, audio, image posts, polls, and Discord roles, plus a member app. At 5% it undercuts Patreon's 10% standard tier. A creator with 1,000 members at $5 grosses $5,000; Fourthwall takes $250 versus Patreon's $500, though card processing adds about $445 on top either way. The angle that compounds is bundling: the same follower who buys a shirt can also join a tier and grab a template.

### 3. Sell Digital Products And Take Tips
List ebooks, Lightroom presets, Notion templates, art packs, or course files. Free plan charges 5% on digital; Pro drops it to 0%. Tips and donations run at 0% on both plans. For creators sitting on a back catalog of downloadable assets, this is the fastest win - upload once, sell forever, no fulfillment.

### 4. Plug Straight Into Where Your Audience Lives
YouTube Merch Shelf, TikTok Shop, Twitch Gifting, and Discord connect natively, so fans buy without leaving the app they follow you on. Email and SMS capture, Zapier, and Kit/Klaviyo/Mailchimp/beehiiv feed the remarketing loop, and you own the list. That last part is the quiet advantage: the data is yours, not rented.

## Where It Beats The Alternatives

Against Patreon, Fourthwall wins on fee (5% vs 10% standard) and adds a real storefront plus POD merch in one place. Against Ko-fi, it matches the 5% but brings a proper shop and fulfillment Fourthwall handles for you. Against Shopify, it removes the monthly subscription and the app stack you'd bolt on for memberships and POD - you start at $0 and pay only when you sell.

The differentiator is the bundled merch plus memberships plus digital plus tips on a single owned domain, with fulfillment taken off your plate. Most rivals make you pick two of those and wire the rest yourself.

## The Honest Downsides

The member 'app' is a mobile web app, not a native App Store app - Fourthwall's help center says so plainly. If you wanted an owned channel in the stores, you don't get one. Merch quality is inconsistent in reviews: wrong colors, print defects, and slow production show up often because outside partners do the printing, and a bad shirt lands on your brand. The 5% membership fee stays on Pro, so scaling memberships doesn't lower that cut. There is no discovery engine - zero organic traffic if you start cold. And support thins out on order problems, worst when a launch is live and customers are messaging you directly.

## Who Should Use It

If you run a YouTube, Twitch, or TikTok audience and want merch, memberships, digital products, and tips under one branded roof with no monthly fee, Fourthwall is the cleanest start I've seen. Start on Free, keep the markup on merch, and move to Pro once digital-product volume makes the 0% cut worth $19/mo. Skip it if you need native app distribution, expect the platform to send buyers, or sell only one $3 digital file where the 5% barely matters. Treat it as your storefront, not your traffic source: bring the audience, and Fourthwall handles the rest.
